It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System The dwarf planet candidate, called ED138, appeared in telescope images and takes roughly 280 years to orbit the sun. Astronomers need to determine its size to properly classify it Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science November 12, 2026 12:00 p.m. Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source The new dwarf planet candidate, called 2026 ED138, orbits on a plane tiled nearly 25 degrees compared to our solar system's main planets, suggesting it was disturbed by gravitational interactions with Neptune. NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor Image Processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Orbit data provided by the IAU Minor Planet Center (MPCorb catalog), funded by NASA PDCO and the Tamkin Foundation. Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC Matthew Holman , a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big. Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.” Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić . They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became. “We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks , he says. The object, called 2026 ED138 , is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system. “This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne , a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.” 2026 ED138 3D orbit Watch on Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides . But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.) Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions. ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger. Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says. Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light. Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.” The Vera C. Rubin Observatory captured the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in these images between March and June this year. NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA Image Processing: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto , Eris , Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.” The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds. What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert. “Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement . “I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb , a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN ’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.” Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood. “Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.” You Might Also Like What Seeded Life on Earth? Â· 3 min read Share Copy link Share on X Share on Bluesky Share on LinkedIn Today, weâre rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency. Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity. Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems. For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static âmodel routerâ that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves. Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks. Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation. Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argonâs 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flashâs 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier. Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text. Getting started Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business . title: Rust 1.100
body_text: Announcing Rust 1.100.0 | Rust Blog Rust Blog Rust Install Learn Tools Governance Community 🖌 Light Dark System Announcing Rust 1.100.0 Nov. 12, 2026 · The Rust Release Team The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup , you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0 . If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel ( rustup default beta ) or the nightly channel ( rustup default nightly ). Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable ! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return , break , and std::process::exit , also have the type ! . Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if : fn mrrrow ( option : Option < u32 > ) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some ( x ) => x , // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return , } ; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions ( -> ! ), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap < T > ( res : Result < T , ! > ) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok ( v ) = res ; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using ! . This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024 . This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it. Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal . A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon! DropGuard : run a closure on every exit path The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return , ? , or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket . Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: use std :: mem :: DropGuard ; use std :: num :: ParseIntError ; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all ( nums : & mut Vec < u32 > , strings : & [ & str ] ) -> Result < ( ) , ParseIntError > { let len = nums . len ( ) ; let mut nums = DropGuard :: new ( nums , move | nums | { nums . truncate ( len ) ; // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure } ) ; for s in strings { nums . push ( s . parse ( ) ? ) ; // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard :: dismiss ( nums ) ; // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok ( ( ) ) } Conjuring zero-sized types As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this. This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst . Instead of transmuting () , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() , or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing. Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it. Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g. warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber` A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml , completing this project goal . See also the other lints that have been introduced . Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees. The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory. This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal , unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking. We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns. You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml : [ registry ] global-min-publish-age = " 3 days " When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back: $ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago) When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update: $ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE = a l l o w cargo update clap - -precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days) The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it. A few things to keep in mind: This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back. cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed. Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would. Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal , including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases. Stitch types Type What it does Works on Fill (tatami) Staggered rows, any angle, with underlay (edge walk + rows) and pull compensation Filled shapes Satin Zigzag column between two rails, with center/contour/zigzag underlay, pull compensation and short stitches on tight curves; plain, S-stitch or zig-zag top stitching; several threads across the column (multicolor satin) Strokes (any width); Ink/Stitch-style two-rail paths with rungs; filled shapes : rings use inner/outer outline, bars/letters/crescents split at their tips (auto-satin), or border follows the outline Run Running stitch, single or triple (bean) Strokes and outlines Contour Rows that follow the outline inward, or one spiral out from the center (Ink/Stitch's circular fill) Filled shapes Blanket E-stitch: a line with prongs into the shape Edges, appliqué Appliqué Placement line → stop → tack-down → stop → satin cover Filled shapes Manual Every path point is a needle point Imported machine files, pen tool Meander One wandering line through the shape, quilting style: light and soft Filled shapes Ripple Open running-stitch rows following the outline, or one spiral Filled shapes Cross-stitch A grid of X's, sewn as rows of half-crosses out and back Filled shapes Tartan Woven stripes in several threads (a mirrored sett you edit in the panel), each thread its own color block Filled shapes Satins wider than 7 mm are auto-split (shorter, staggered stitches) and use auto spacing (narrow columns more open, wide ones denser). Planner features: Remove overlaps: fill hidden under later objects isn't sewn (keeps 0.5 mm of overlap). Cap order: center-out, bottom-up, grouped by color, still respecting layering. Routing: travel stitches stay out of sight: straight across where a straight line stays inside the fill, otherwise round the inside of its outline (Ink/Stitch's underpath), otherwise any way through the fill (round its holes, through its necks) or under whatever is sewn later on top. A fill in separate parts is sewn part by part, each part's underlay and top together. So a fill with cut-outs, or a dither in scattered blocks under another color, is sewn with few or no cuts. Trims only where none of that works (up to 50 mm of travel). Sewing control per object: a start and an end point (where the thread comes in and leaves, so the next object is close), trim after, stop after (to lay foam or trim appliqué). What's left to cut is the document's Connect bar: drag it to sew across gaps up to N mm (between objects, or the parts of one) with running stitches instead of cuts. Those stitches show, so the panel counts the cuts saved as you drag and the canvas lights up what would be sewn. Fabric presets: standard, thin cotton cap, structured cap, knit. Checks: narrow fills, wide/narrow satins, small lettering, tiny gaps, fully covered objects, hoop fit. Group colors: reorder to cut thread changes without breaking layering. Mac app On a Mac with Rust and the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ): packaging/macos/make-app.sh --install # builds ZigZag.app and copies it to /Applications packaging/macos/make-app.sh --dmg # also makes dist/ZigZag-<version>.dmg to share packaging/macos/make-app.sh --universal # one app for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs packaging/macos/make-app.sh --release # the DMG to publish: universal, signed, notarized --release signs with your Developer ID and has Apple notarize the app and the DMG, so it opens on any Mac without warnings. Once, beforehand: add a Developer ID Application certificate (Xcode › Settings › Accounts › Manage Certificates › +), make an app-specific password at account.apple.com, and save the notarization credentials in your keychain: xcrun notarytool store-credentials zigzag-notary --apple-id YOUR_APPLE_ID --team-id YOUR_TEAM_ID The app bundles the studio, the zigzag command-line tool and the MCP bridge. To use the command line from anywhere: ln -s /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag /usr/local/bin/zigzag . For Claude Desktop, point the MCP config at /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag-mcp . Without --release the app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. It opens normally on the Mac that built it. On another Mac, macOS blocks it the first time: open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open instead). macOS asks for Bluetooth permission the first time you send to the Skitch. Studio The approved embroidered icons live in packaging/macos/AppIcon.png (light) and packaging/macos/AppIcon-dark.png (dark). The Mac build regenerates both multi-resolution .icns files; run bash packaging/macos/make-icons.sh to regenerate them separately. Finder and the unopened app use the light icon. While the studio is running, its Dock icon follows the app's light/dark theme, including the ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark override. zigzag-studio [design.svg | logo.png] [--mcp-port 7878 | --no-mcp | --mcp-stdio] Laid out like Illustrator, styled like a Mac app: Tools down the left edge: Select (V), Direct Selection (A), Hand (H), Pen (P): click for corners, drag for curves (Option breaks the handles, Shift keeps 45°, Space moves the point being placed); while drawing, Option lends it the Anchor Point tool (drag a segment to bend it, a handle to move it alone, click a smooth point for a corner) and ⌘ lends Direct Selection (drag a point or handle, then keep drawing), and on a selected path Option-drag bends a segment too. Illustrator's Pen group is behind it: Add Anchor Point (+) clicks a point onto an outline without changing its shape, Delete Anchor Point (-) clicks one out (Option swaps the two while held), and Anchor Point (Shift+C) converts points between smooth and corner and drags one handle alone. Press and hold the Pen (or right-click it) for the group's flyout, Option-click it to step through the group, or tear the group off into a toolbar of its own with the strip at the flyout's edge; the Shape tools work the same way. Brush (B), with VectorCraft's path clean-up tools in its group: Smooth (drag along a path to take the wobble out: fewer points, smoother curves; Smoothness in the bar above), Path Eraser (drag across a path to cut that part away) and Join (scrub between two open ends to join them, or an open path's two ends to close it). Shapes (M rectangle, L ellipse, \ line; hold or right-click for polygon and star), Fill Angle (G), Measure (I), Text (T). Below them, the selection's thread swatch: click it for the thread color picker. Curves, the Illustrator way: the Pen clicks corners and click-drags curves (Option while dragging breaks the handle for a sharp turn; Shift keeps points and handles at 45°; hold Space to move the point you're placing). Click the last point to make it a corner, or drag from it to start the next curve in a new direction. Click the first point to close a shape; Enter, Esc, ⌘-click or another tool ends a line and keeps it. With a path selected, the Pen continues it from an open end, adds a point on its outline, deletes a point you click, and Option-click turns a point corner ↔ smooth (Option-drag pulls out new handles). While drawing, click another open path's end to join the two into one. The cursor shows what a click will do. Direct Selection drags points and handles of any shape from your SVG (circles and rects become paths); dragging a curve bends it under the pointer (Option-drag bends a straight one; a plain drag moves it); Delete removes points, arrows nudge them. Smart guides while drawing (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U): Pen points, shape corners and dragged points land on other objects' anchors and centers, where two outlines cross, on an outline, on 45° rays from the last point (level and upright handles too), or in line with any of those, with a magenta label saying which ("anchor", "intersect", "path", "align"…). With Shift, a point keeps its 45° angle and slides into line with the nearest target. Round corners: in Direct Selection a small circle sits inside each sharp corner; drag it in to round the corners (the selected points', or all of them), each only as far as its sides allow. Object › Path › Round Corners… does the same with a radius and Round, Inverted or Chamfer, previewed live. Brush (B), after Illustrator's Paintbrush: paint a line freehand and it comes out smooth, sewn as a satin column at the width you set (or as a running stitch). Smoothness takes out the hand's wobble; sharp turns stay sharp; end where you began to close the line. The cursor is a circle as wide as the satin. Shapes, the Illustrator way: Rectangle (M), Ellipse (L), Polygon, Star and Line (\). Drag from a corner; Option draws from the center, Shift makes a square or circle, keeps a polygon or star upright and a line at 45°. While dragging a polygon or star, ↑/↓ add or remove sides or points. Click without dragging to type an exact size. The bar at the top of the canvas switches shapes and sets corner radius, sides, points and the star's inner radius. Closed shapes come in as fills, lines as runs, in the current thread. Path tools: Object › Pathfinder (Unite, Minus Front, Intersect, Exclude; also buttons in the Transform panel when two or more objects are selected) and Object › Path (Offset Path…, Outline Stroke, Simplify…, Round Corners…, Clean Up…). Simplify… is VectorCraft's slider, from fewest points to closest to the original, previewed live, with Auto-Simplify picking the level for the selection's size. Clean Up… removes stray points, objects too small to sew (under 1 mm by default) and extra points (points on top of each other, points in the middle of straight lines), showing how many of each it found first. Results come back as smooth curves with their real corners (least-squares curve fitting), not as many-sided polygons. Logos from images (Image Trace): open, drop or place a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF and the Trace Image window traces it into flat-color shapes, previewed on your hat's color. Choose how many colors (or Auto), the width, detail and the smallest speck to keep; remove the white background; snap every color to your Brother, Janome or own palette's threads; and sew thin lines as single lines. Flat logos trace exactly (edges placed to a fraction of a pixel, corners restored, circles and straight lines exact); photos are posterized. The command line traces too: zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes . Contextual task bar: under the selection, the next things you'd do: its stitch type, its thread, Edit Points, Round Corners, Simplify, Unite (two or more), Duplicate. View › Contextual Task Bar (or its ••• menu) hides it. Ask an agent: the Agent panel (full height in the left dock; the sparkle at the bottom of the tool strip opens and closes it, and ⌘K or Window › Ask Agent… opens it with the prompt ready) runs Claude Code or Codex in the background, connected to this studio's MCP server, so you watch it build the design. It can only use the design tools (no shell, no file edits). The transcript shows what it said and each step, with a spinner on the one running (the one place it's shown; collapse the panel and its header shows the step and the time instead). On the canvas, the objects it's working on get a moving outline, a shimmer and a label saying what it's doing (Drawing, Placing, Restyling…), for any agent connected over MCP, not just the panel's. The panel is named for the agent (Claude Code or Codex; switch in its ≡ menu); + in its header starts a new chat, Stop ends a run. Uses the claude or codex command you've already signed in to. Like any panel it can float, join another as a tab or dock right; sharing a dock it sits at the bottom, under a divider you drag to give it more room. Thread colors and palettes: the picker shows the nearest Brother/Janome thread, a palette to click (Brother, Janome or your own), and a small custom color field. Make palettes from scratch, from the design, or from a thread kit you own (the palette's ≡ menu › New Palette from Thread Kit: Brother's 12, 40 and 22 color sets, or 40 + 22 for all 61; then Match All keeps a design to the threads in your box), add the selection's thread with +, right-click to remove; they're remembered between launches. Threads panel: the design's threads in sewing order (each color block numbered, with its stitches, and "stop" where the same thread comes twice running) or By Color (each thread once, with how many objects use it). Click a row to select what it sews; click a swatch to change that block's thread, or in By Color that thread everywhere. Group Colors and the count of color changes and trims are under the list. The panel's ≡ menu has Match All to the chosen palette, and Show Palette puts a palette to click under the list (off by default, since the thread picker has the same palettes). Panels, the Illustrator way: the Agent has the left dock to itself; Objects, Stitch, Transform, Lettering, Threads and Document are on the right. The design's issues are in the status bar (bottom right): a warning sign with a count, or a check when all's well; click it (or Window › Issues) for the list, each linked to its object. Drag a panel by its header to reorder it, move it to the other dock, or drop it on the canvas to float it (each panel's ≡ menu also has Dock Left / Dock Right / Float). Drop a panel on another panel's header and they share it as tabs; drag a tab out (or use Separate in the ≡ menu) to part them, drag the header to move the group. » at the top of a dock collapses it to a strip of icons for a bigger canvas: click an icon and the panel flies out beside the strip (drag an icon to move that panel). Click a header to collapse a panel; Window › Reset Panels puts everything back. The layout is remembered. Tabs, one per document (as in VectorCraft and Illustrator): Open, drop or New opens a file in a tab of its own over the canvas (the empty document you start with makes way for the first one); a file that's already open just comes forward. Each tab keeps its own undo history, selection, zoom and stitches. Click a tab to switch, ⌃Tab / ⌃⇧Tab (or Window › Next / Previous Document) to step through them, drag one to reorder, middle-click or its × (or File › Close, ⌘W) to close it; + opens a new document and » lists every tab when they don't all fit. A dot in place of the × marks unsaved changes, and closing such a tab asks whether to save it first. Right-click a tab for Close Other Tabs and Copy Path. Quitting doesn't ask: every tab comes back next time, each with its unsaved changes. Menu bar (File, Edit, Object, View, Window) with the usual ⌘ shortcuts. It's the real macOS menu bar on a Mac, drawn in the window elsewhere. Cursors drawn for each tool: the Pen's nib (with what a click will do), crosshairs for the Shape, Measure and Fill Angle tools, Direct Selection's hollow arrow, and a curved arrow at rotate corners. Right-click menus on the canvas and the Objects list, styled like the tool flyouts: the stitch types with their icons, then the usual commands with their shortcuts. Stays quick on big designs: stitches are planned once per change, reusing every object that didn't change (overlap removal too: moving one object redoes only the objects it overlaps); a design that takes more than 12 ms to plan plans in the background (the status bar says "Updating stitches…" and the last plan stays on screen meanwhile; when you drop a moved object its stitches move with it until the new plan lands). Dragging points or objects, and typing, preview without re-planning until you let go. The stitches live on the GPU: each color block's segments are uploaded once and drawn by a shader (thread shading and needle points included), so panning, zooming, dragging and the stitch player cost nothing per stitch on the CPU, whether the design has a thousand stitches or half a million. The Objects list lays out only the rows in view. An object whose stitches hit an internal error is left out with a warning in Issues rather than taking the plan down. For development: TL_PROFILE=1 prints each frame's sections to stderr, TL_NO_GPU=1 draws the stitches with the painter instead, and cargo test --release --features gui --bin zigzag-studio perf_bench -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 times typing and dragging on a traced logo ( examples/bench-grid.svg is a 213,000-stitch design for the studio itself). Follows the system's light or dark appearance ( ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark overrides) and uses the San Francisco system font on a Mac. Pick a stitch type per object: big buttons, the task bar, right-click, or F/S/R/C/X (Blanket and Manual from the Stitch panel). The preview re-plans live. Layout, the Illustrator way: drag to move (Shift: 45° steps; Option: drag a copy). Handles resize freely (Shift keeps proportions, Option resizes from the center, drag past the far side to flip); just outside a corner rotates (Shift: 45°). Smart guides snap edges and centers to other objects and the hoop (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U). ⌘D is Transform Again: Option-drag a copy, then ⌘D for more at the same spacing. Hold Space to pan with any tool (a tap plays the stitch-out). The Transform panel has Illustrator's reference point: X/Y show the chosen point and W/H resize around it. Also rotate, flip, center in hoop, fit to hoop (artwork bigger than the hoop is scaled down to fit when you open or place it; Undo restores full size), ⌘C/⌘V, arrows nudge 0.5 mm (Shift 5 mm). Edits are saved as SVG transforms. Groups work like Illustrator: a click or drag takes the whole group; double-click goes into it (the rest dims and a breadcrumb shows where you are), double-click again to go deeper; Esc or double-click on empty canvas comes back out. ⌘-click picks one object without going in. Layers (Illustrator's "Layer 1", Inkscape layers, Figma frames) aren't groups. Copy, paste and duplicate keep groups. Type (T), as in VectorCraft and Illustrator: click where the text should go and type straight onto the canvas (Enter for a new line, Esc or a click elsewhere when done); click text, or between its letters, to edit it with the caret where you clicked (or double-click it with the Selection tool, which picks text anywhere in its box and shows it as a box, not its letters' points; delete every letter and finish, and the text is removed) (←/→, ↑/↓, Home/End and ⌘←/→ move it; Backspace and Delete remove either side; Shift with any of those, a drag, a double-click for a word, a triple-click or ⌘A for the lot selects text, which typing replaces and ⌘C/⌘X/⌘V copy, cut and paste); click a selected path to put text on it. The Lettering panel is a compact Character panel (hat text isn't long copy): font (with search), bold/italic, letter height, tracking, pair kerning (pick the pair, or Option+←/→ while typing kerns the pair at the caret), horizontal and vertical scale, case (as typed, UPPER, lower, Title), alignment and leading for two-line text, baseline (straight, arc over, arc under, or on a path with offset and flip), and the stitch type. The Type menu has Type on a Path, Change Case, Align and Create Outlines (⇧⌘O). Text is a shape like any other: Direct Selection, Round Corners, Simplify, Pathfinder and Clean Up all work on it (it quietly becomes plain paths at the first point-level edit, one undo step), and it saves as real SVG text until then. Pen (P): draw filled shapes or lines with corners and curves, or place manual stitches one by one. Snaps to the grid when it's showing, else to smart guides. Shapes (M, L, \): rectangles (with rounded corners), ellipses, polygons, stars and lines. Measure , mm grid , needle points , First/Last , Group colors . Open machine files (PES, PEC, DST, EXP, JEF) to view, resize and re-export them, and images to trace. Settings per type: fill angle (with a drag-to-set angle tool , A ), spacing, length, pull, underlay. Satin options: column vs border, stitch (satin, S-stitch, zig-zag), threads across the column, width, underlay passes, short stitches. Contour and ripple: rings or spiral. Cross-stitch: cell size. Tartan: the stripes (color and width each, mirrored), angle, row spacing. Run options: single or triple. Sewing row in the Stitch panel: Start and End (click the outline; green and red markers you can drag), Trim and Stop after the object. Edit › Copy / Paste Stitch Settings carries one object's type and settings to others (each keeps its thread and start/end); Edit › Select Same Stitch Type; Object › Path › Reverse Direction sews a path from its other end. Test swatches (Object › Test Swatches…): copies of the selection in a grid, one setting (spacing, length, pull compensation, satin width, fill angle) stepped from a value to another, each lettered with its value, to stitch out and compare on the real fabric. View › Density Map tints where stitches pile up (yellow from 2.5 per mm², red at 4), and View › Sewing Order numbers the objects on the canvas. Fabric preset, hoop, Remove overlaps and Cap order in the Document panel. Preview on your hat's color. Issues list (status bar): problems link to the object. Satins show their rails on the canvas. Sewing order: Earlier/Later. Stitch player (Space). Undo/redo everything. Save (Ctrl/⌘ S) writes settings into the SVG; Export PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC/PEN or a worksheet (HTML: picture, size, time, every color stop with the nearest Brother and Janome thread); Send to Skitch . Measuring and units. Measure (I) works like VectorCraft's: drag between two points to read the distance, angle, width and height. The ends snap to points, edges and the hoop (or to the grid when it's on), Shift keeps the line to 45°, and the reading stays until the next drag (Escape clears it). View › Units, or the unit menu in the status bar, shows sizes, positions, distances and the grid in millimeters, centimeters, inches, points or pixels (SVG pixels, 1/96 in, as files are read); it's remembered between launches. Any length field also takes a typed unit or a sum ( 1/4 in , 25.4mm , 10+5 ). The grid (⌘') follows the unit, inches in halves down to 1/32, and labels its major lines along the canvas's top and left edges from the hoop's center. Stitch settings (spacing, density, pull compensation) stay in millimeters. Picks up where you left off. Quit (or crash) and reopen: the same files come back, every tab with any unsaved changes, the zoom and the selection, and the same tab in front. Changes are kept as you work ( session.json and one recovery file per tab, recovery.svg , recovery-2.svg …, in ZigZag's settings folder ( ~/Library/Application Support/ZigZag ), each written whole or not at all), never written into your file until you save. Opening the app with a file skips this. If the app went down while bringing a document back, the next launch keeps it aside as recovery-crashed.svg instead of trying again (and an unreadable one as recovery-unreadable.svg ), and says so in the status bar. A job on the Skitch comes back too: the design last sent is kept ( sent.json ), the Skitch window reopens if it was open and reconnects, and once the machine reports that design its progress shows on it again (the machine keeps the design and where the needle is; Stop ends the job on both). Agents (MCP) The studio runs an MCP server on http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp (Streamable HTTP, localhost only, Origin-checked). Agents edit the live document you're looking at (the tab in front), and every call is one undo step. MCP in the status bar (bottom right, next to the Skitch) shows whether agents can reach the studio: a gray dot while it waits, green once a client has connected, blue and pulsing while calls come in, red if the server couldn't start. Click it for the address, the commands to connect Claude Code and Claude Desktop (with Copy buttons), the clients that have connected, the recent tool calls (failed ones in red, with the error on hover) and the tools on offer. Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp Claude Desktop / stdio clients ( claude_desktop_config.json ): { "mcpServers" : { "zigzag" : { "command" : " /path/to/zigzag-mcp " } } } zigzag-mcp forwards to the running studio. Use --port N if you changed it. With "args": ["--headless"] it works without the app open: the same tools on a document no one is watching ( zigzag-studio --mcp-stdio ), kept only when the agent saves or exports it. Tools: get_design , add_svg (place/scale artwork in mm), set_object , delete_object , move_object transform_objects (size, scale, rotate, mirror, move), duplicate_objects add_text , edit_text , list_fonts set_document (fabric, hoop, overlaps, cap order, preview color), group_colors render_preview (returns a PNG of the stitches), check_design , get_svg , select open_file (SVG, machine file or image, in a tab of its own), list_documents , switch_document , new_document , undo , save , export (machine formats or html worksheet), send_to_skitch , machine_status trace_image (PNG/JPEG logo → shapes, colors snapped to a thread chart), round_corners , simplify (VectorCraft's 0–100 levels, or Auto), clean_up batch : several calls in one, all or nothing and one undo step; later steps can use earlier results ( "$0.added.0.name" ) Arguments a tool doesn't take are refused with the ones it does (a misspelt widht_mm isn't silently ignored), and each tool says whether it only reads. Outline text, or it falls back to system fonts. Opening the ZigZag-saved SVG back in Illustrator keeps the settings in the layer names. Name layers or objects to set their stitching. Illustrator's _x3D_ -style escapes are decoded, and group settings apply to everything inside the group. Token Meaning fill satin run skip stitch type a=45 fill angle (degrees) s=0.3 row / zigzag spacing (mm) l=3 max stitch length (mm) pc=0.2 pull compensation (mm per side) w=3 satin width (mm) border satin along a filled shape's outline instead of across it u=0 underlay off ul=center+contour+zigzag satin underlay passes ( ul=none ) ss=0 short stitches off r=3 running passes (3 = bean) contour blanket applique manual the other stitch types split=7 satin auto-split length (mm); split=0 off t=e8a33c thread color override o=2 sewing order stroke.… applies only to the stroke of an object that also has a fill, e.g. stroke.run Example layer names: logo fill a=45 s=0.35 , title satin , outline stroke.satin stroke.w=1.5 . Skitch over Bluetooth The Skitch window (the toolbar's Send button or File › Send to Skitch…) runs the whole job, like a slicer's device page follows a print: the design on the left, what to do on the right, and the steps across the top (Connect · Home · Send · Trial · Sew · Done). Connect and pair. It scans for the Skitch. The first time, hold the Skitch's Bluetooth button until it beeps, then Connect (or Try Again); if the computer asks to pair, accept. On a Mac the Skitch never appears in System Settings › Bluetooth (it's a Bluetooth LE device): it pairs when ZigZag connects. Allow ZigZag to use Bluetooth if macOS asks (Privacy & Security › Bluetooth). Close Artspira first: the Skitch talks to one app at a time. Home. A machine just turned on asks to be homed (frame off, Accept, frame back on); the window shows the steps and moves on when it's done. Send: the hoop with the design where it will sew: As Placed (where it sits in the studio's hoop, so you can put it high on a cap) or Centered ; the threads to have ready, in sewing order, by Brother Embroidery name and number; a "before you sew" checklist; Send Design. Trial run (Brother's name for it; on by default after sending): press Accept on the machine and the needle goes around the design's outline without sewing, so you can check it clears the frame's magnets, seams and the brim. Trial Again whenever you rehoop. Sew: Start, then press Start on the machine. The picture shows what's sewn, faded where it hasn't been yet, with the needle and the thread on now; under it, a timeline of the threads with the needle's place. The side shows progress, time left, the thread on now and the next one, and at each thread change exactly which thread to put on. The canvas and the status bar follow along too. Start / Pause / Stop. Start (or Resume, or Sew Again) readies the machine; Pause is the Skitch's own Start/Stop button (it can't be paused over Bluetooth); Stop ends the job, taking the design off the machine. While paused, drag along the timeline or step the needle by 1, 10 or 100 stitches or back to the thread's start, then Resume. Errors say what they are and what to do (thread breaks, bobbin, needle plate, frame). After a thread break the needle goes back over the gap (6 stitches for the top thread, 2 for the bobbin, as Artspira does). Minimize it (–) to keep working while it stitches: the canvas is your design again, and the machine's icon at the right of the status bar shows what it's doing and how far, with a small bar (click it to bring the window back). The window comes back by itself when the machine needs you: a thread change, an error, or the end. The ••• menu also links to Brother's Skitch how-to videos (threading, the bobbin, the frame, a thread break, tension, cleaning). The window's ••• menu can connect to a simulated machine , which does each step on the machine by itself, to try it all without a Skitch. Agents can send_to_skitch and follow along with machine_status . The protocol was reverse-engineered (see NOTICE), so avoid firmware updates. Working out undocumented commands Thread tension isn't a Bluetooth setting on the Skitch: it's the tension dial on the machine. Speed is fixed (about 400 stitches a minute). The machine does report a block of settings, and Artspira has a settings screen, so two tools are here for working out what else it can do: Settings bytes (in the Skitch window, under the machine's details): reads the settings block the machine reports. Read it, disconnect, change one setting in Artspira, close Artspira, reconnect and read again: the bytes that changed are marked. Every read is kept in skitch-settings.log beside the panel layout. On the command line: zigzag skitch settings --label "what changed" --log settings.log . zigzag capture FILE lists the Skitch conversation in a Bluetooth recording of Artspira, by command name, with changed settings bytes in [brackets] ( --all for the upload and polling too, --raw for every ATT operation). It reads both: iPhone: install Apple's Bluetooth logging profile on the phone (developer.apple.com › Bug Reporting › Profiles and Logs), restart it, plug it into the Mac, and in PacketLogger (Apple's Additional Tools for Xcode ) choose File › New iOS Trace; save the trace ( .pklg ). Android: Developer options › Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, then adb bugreport and take btsnoop_hci.log from it. Writing settings stays out of ZigZag until a layout is known and a write of the machine's own settings, unchanged, reads back the same. Ink/Stitch parity Checked against Ink/Stitch 's features and tool docs: Ink/Stitch ZigZag Running, bean, manual stitch; satin column (two rails with rungs), E-stitch; tatami, contour, circular (spiral) fill ✓ Ripple, meander, cross-stitch and tartan fills; S-stitch, zigzag and multicolor satin ✓ Params per object with fabric-aware defaults; start/end commands; trim and stop commands ✓ (Stitch panel's Sewing row) Auto-route (travel inside fills, underpath along the outline, under what's sewn on top), Jump to Stroke ✓ (document's Connect bar) Simulator, stitch plan preview, density map, stacking-order labels ✓ Lettering (system fonts, arcs, text on a path, multi-line, case, scale), thread palettes, Match All, thread kits ✓ (Brother and Janome charts) Duplicate params, select by type, flip satin direction, test swatches, cleanup, troubleshoot (Issues) ✓ Import stitch files and edit at stitch level; PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC ✓ Gradient fill, guided fill; redwork, cutwork; pre-digitized fonts; 60+ thread brands; PDF print not yet Hatch parity Checked against Wilcom Hatch's core feature set: Hatch ZigZag Tatami, satin, run/triple run, contour fill, blanket, appliqué, manual stitches ✓ Auto underlay, pull compensation, auto spacing, satin auto-split, short stitches ✓ Fabric settings that set densities and compensation ✓ (4 presets) Lettering with TrueType fonts, straight, arc and path baselines, typed on the canvas ✓ (system fonts) Select, move, resize, rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy/paste, align to hoop ✓ Digitize shapes and manual stitches by hand ✓ (pen tool) Remove overlaps, color sequencing, re-order objects ✓ Stitch player, show needle points, grid, measure ✓ Open and save PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3 ✓ (VP3 write only) Production worksheet ✓ (HTML) Auto-digitize bitmaps ✓ (Image Trace: flat logos, posterized photos, centre lines) Built-in embroidery fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif/pattern fills, 3D foam not yet Status Verified: 136 library tests, 153 editor/MCP tests (UI interactions via egui_kittest, a full agent workflow, a real HTTP JSON-RPC session, atomic batches, the Skitch flow against a simulated machine), with and without Bluetooth built in, plus the 222 tests of the vendored Image Trace. Every writer (PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3) reads back through pyembroidery with identical stitch positions; our readers read pyembroidery-written files. PEN output checked against hand-computed sequences. Studio run on Mesa OpenGL and driven by an agent over MCP. Tested on a real Brother Skitch (PP1). Screenshots and videos Start the studio with ZIGZAG_CAPTURE=<folder> and ⌃⌥⌘S saves the window as a full-resolution PNG; ⌃⌥⌘R starts and stops recording it. packaging/media/encode.sh <folder>/take-001 demo turns a recording into demo.mp4 and demo.gif (needs ffmpeg). Credits See NOTICE , and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md for the licenses of the libraries ZigZag is built from (regenerate it with packaging/licenses/generate.sh after changing dependencies). PES/PEC/DST layouts and the Brother palette are from pyembroidery (MIT). Image Trace is vendored from VectorCraft (MIT OR Apache-2.0), whose curve fitting, live corners, snap targets and colour difference were also ported (see vendor/README.md ). Tatami, satin and short-stitch approaches follow Ink/Stitch . About Free, open-source embroidery software for Mac and Windows. TV boxes, old tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself. Two devices so far 📺 Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen) 📱 iPad Air (2013) Chip Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 Apple A7, 2 cores RAM 1.9 GB (about 1 GB usable) 1 GB (about 700 MB usable) OS Android 14, no root iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken Everyday model Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) at 24-26 tok/s Biggest model Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 5.1 tok/s Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 2.6-4.5 tok/s Full results docs/tv-box.md ipad-air/README.md Both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash as it's needed. More devices (phones, single-board computers, routers) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM. How it works All of it is a patch on llama.cpp . The main ideas: Kernels built for the chip. A 1-bit lookup-table kernel, repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the Cortex-A55, and versions of them for the A7, which has no dot-product instructions. Less RAM per model. Most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so we drop those output rows. On the TV, a "headless" mode also stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs. Experts paged from flash. A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token. We keep the popular ones in RAM, read the others from flash on demand and prefetch the next layer's. This is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB. Streaming for dense models bigger than RAM, at the flash's full speed. docs/how-it-works.md has every technique with its measured gain. Try it The quickest start is a ready-made model file from Hugging Face. They need the patched llama.cpp: stock llama.cpp can't load them. TV box or another ARMv8.2 Android device: docs/tv-box-setup.md Jailbroken iPad on iOS 12: ipad-air/README.md All model files and how to rebuild them: docs/models.md Read more Page What's in it docs/tv-box.md device #1: every model run on the TV box, speed and quality ipad-air/README.md device #2: the iPad Air results, setup and scripts docs/how-it-works.md the kernels, memory tricks, expert pager and streaming engine docs/models.md downloads for both devices, rebuild targets and checksums docs/lessons.md what we learned, including what didn't work EXPERIMENT.md the full lab notebook: 160 experiments, failures included What's in the repo Path What patches/ every change to llama.cpp for the TV box (the iPad's patch is in ipad-air/patches/ ) tools/ model rebuilding, GGUF rewriting, benchmarks and kernel checks tv-llm-ui/ the live token-stream chat page and its launcher ipad-air/ device #2: iOS 12 build, smolchat , deploy and benchmark scripts bench/ every chat benchmark ( results.jsonl ) and the raw logs data/ vocabulary lists and evaluation texts tiny-llm-web/ the first experiment: a 260K-parameter story model zigcc/ zig wrappers for cross-compiling static aarch64 binaries Star History License MIT . title: Abandoned Quake 4 expansion finished by modders and now playable
body_text: openq4 0.14.1 windows x64 file - ModDB Hello guest register or sign in   or with: openq4 0.14.1 windows x64 file HOME Today Week Month Year games popular latest indies publishing add game mods popular latest add mod addons popular latest upload files popular latest upload RTX Remix Games Compatibility Remix Mods Remix Files PBR Assets News Tutorials Statistics videos images audio articles reviews headlines blogs post article engines popular latest add engine developers popular latest add dev groups popular latest add group forums jobs post job openQ4 Quake 4 mod | Released Sep 18, 2026 summary articles reviews files videos images openQ4 is a free, open-source engine and game-code replacement for Quake 4. Play the original campaign and multiplayer on today's Windows, Linux and Steam Deck, with widescreen support, smooth high-refresh motion and optional visual upgrades. Add file Report openq4 0.14.1 windows x64 Location Games : Quake 4 : Mods : openQ4 : Files Filename openq4-0.14.1-windows-x64.zip Category Full Version Uploader themuffinman86 Added Nov 11th, 2026 Size 648.86mb (680,374,349 bytes) Downloads 187 (20 today) MD5 Hash 665488382e34a7d9b3dcd33d355dff04 Embed Button Embed Widget 648.86mb Download Now Description openQ4 0.14.1, the Awakening Edition: play the recovered Quake 4 expansion beside the original campaign, with stable shadow mapping, a new interface, Vulkan on Windows, smarter bots and an experimental Android app. The Quake 4 expansion that never shipped is now playable. openQ4 0.14.1, the Awakening Edition , is out now, and it is the biggest update since 0.13.2. It brings a second campaign, stable shadow mapping, a rebuilt interface, Vulkan on Windows, smarter bots and an experimental Android app, then spends the extra weeks polishing all of it toward production quality. 0.14.0 was withdrawn soon after release, so for most of you this is the first look at everything below. 0.14.1 replaces it, with every 0.14 feature refined, fixed and optimized. It is a big step on the road to 1.0. The Awakening, at last Raven Software and Ritual Entertainment built an expansion for Quake 4 that was never released. Justin Marshall recovered and published it, and openQ4 now plays it beside the original campaign: pick Single Player &gt; Campaign and choose Quake 4 or The Awakening. All 13 maps on openQ4's own code. The expansion's monsters, weapons and vehicles are rebuilt in openQ4's engine and game code. openQ4 never loads the alpha's game DLL. Finished where the alpha wasn't. Where the alpha's own code or content stopped something working as designed, openQ4 fixes it: the Valkaryne finale, the beach's death-ray turret, the Pain Lord's weak spot and Retches that could never move are the biggest examples. New toys. A chaingun turret with heat and its own HUD, and vehicle HUDs in both the new and classic interfaces. Two campaigns, kept apart. Each keeps its own saves and settings, and returning to Quake 4, Arena or multiplayer removes the expansion's overrides. openQ4 ships none of the expansion's content; you supply the files. The Awakening guide shows how. Looks better, runs faster Shadow mapping you can leave on. The Quality and Ultra presets cast soft, stable shadow maps on OpenGL and Vulkan, with sharp contact shadows that soften with distance. They are cached while lights and casters stay still, so they cost less every frame and no longer shimmer as you walk. The flashlight casts shadows on every preset that draws them. Vulkan on Windows is now supported and the automatic choice for new installs. It was tested across every stock single-player map and 20 multiplayer maps, picks your GPU in Settings, recovers from driver resets, and falls back to OpenGL in the same launch if it has to. Presets re-tiered by frame rate. Ultra now plays smoothly instead of asking for everything at once; the old everything-on Ultra lives on as Maximum . New Low and Enhanced tiers fill the gaps, and Minimum and Low Power suit weak or battery-powered hardware. Smarter Auto-Detect reads your active GPU, memory, resolution and CPU, and fresh installs use it automatically. No more restarts. V-Sync, MSAA, texture quality, window and fullscreen changes and most presets apply to the running game. Quicker loading. Maps load faster, sounds decode in the background, declarations parse a fifth faster and start-up is over a second quicker. Cleaner motion. Temporal AA rebuilds full detail below native resolution and holds still when nothing moves, motion blur looks the same at any frame rate, and cutscenes, cameras, ragdolls and spectating stay smooth on high-refresh screens. A whole new interface The Remastered HUD with Minimal, Competitive and Classic layouts, controller button prompts, and Reduced Motion and Reduced Flashing options. Rebuilt menus and tabbed settings, including a Display page that keeps or reverts a change on a countdown, plus New Game and Chapters pages for the campaigns. Vector weapon wheels and scopes for Marine and Strogg, with live ammo. Animated crosshairs. Each weapon's original crosshair assembles, kicks, charges and reloads with the weapon. Built for every screen: controllers, touch, portrait and tall layouts, and text up to 200%. Arena regains its ceremony: the match-start camera move and "Fight!", opponent introductions and a real pause menu. Prefer the original look? The classic screens and HUD are one setting away: seta ui_retained 0 . Multiplayer, bots and demos Your inputs reach the server on time again, and prediction and lag compensation no longer correct the same delay twice. Bots that take orders. They plan safer routes, hear the fight, time item respawns and follow commands such as everyone follow me . They also stop knocking team-mates off walkways, swim to underwater routes and escape napalm and grenades. Talk to your team: quick chat on D-pad Down or V, push-to-talk voice chat with per-player mute, and objective markers for flags, assault points and DeadZone zones. Demos you can navigate. Multi-view demos gain kill, capture and round markers, Auto-Track and near-instant seeking, and you can record a whole campaign, level transitions included, as one demo. Hosting works as set: Create Server options take effect, the Admin page accepts remote-console passwords, dedicated servers change maps faster, and networking is hardened throughout. Sound and languages Room reverb for every map, as the original game had with EAX hardware: closed doors muffle, hangars boom and radio chatter stays dry. Truer audio: sound variety, stereo width, radio levels and distance falloff now match the original game, and unplugging your headphones no longer cuts the music. Dialogue subtitles with size, backing and speaker names, plus a separate Dialogue Volume. Six new languages: German, Brazilian Portuguese, Czech, Hungarian, Turkish and Ukrainian menus and game text. New frontiers (experimental) Android: a signed ARM64 APK with touch controls, portrait play and a touch layout editor, built on Emile Belanger's port and OpenGL ES renderer. VR: head-tracked stereo through OpenXR, with motion-controller aiming, room-scale movement and comfort options, now on Vulkan too. Level editor: edit brushes, patches and entities in 2D and 3D views, then build and play the map in one click. For modders and mappers: physically based materials with reflection probes, recompiled maps that keep their AI cover positions, and clip brushes that block what they were built to block. Sturdier under the hood Three code audits and static analysis fixed crash, memory-safety and save-restore defects throughout the engine and game code. Saves are now written in a portable format and reported only once they are safely on disk, and openQ4's own data ships as separate packs so future patches can be small downloads. Before you install You need your own copy of Quake 4 from Steam or GOG. openQ4 finds it on its own. Install into a fresh folder. 0.14.1 repacks openQ4's own data, so don't copy it over an older openQ4. Your settings, bindings and saves carry over. Reapply your preset in Settings &gt; System to get the re-tiered values. New saves use a format older builds can't read, so back up your saves if you might go back. Multiplayer needs matching openQ4 0.14.1 clients and servers. Retail Quake 4 and mods built for its original game DLLs are not compatible. Mappers: recompile maps that use vehicle, fly, shot or item clip brushes. Experimental means experimental: VR has not yet been qualified on headset hardware, Android has been qualified on one phone so far, and The Awakening is built from unfinished alpha content, with full playthrough qualification still in progress. Your reports help. Download Grab it from the openQ4 downloads here on ModDB, or get any package from the GitHub release page : Windows x64, as an installer or a zip Linux x64, as an AppImage or an archive (also used on Steam Deck) macOS on Apple Silicon (preview); signed builds are also offered by Mac Source Ports Linux ARM64 (preview), Windows ARM64 and Android ARM64 (experimental) The full release notes list everything new since 0.13.2, with upgrade notes and known limitations. The road to 1.0 0.14.1 is a deliberate push toward 1.0: fewer new experiments and more polish on what already exists. The same engine work now underpins the rebased openPREY and openD3 projects, which share fixes with openQ4 in both directions. Thank you to Emile Belanger for the Android port, Justin Marshall for recovering and publishing The Awakening, Schnapple of Mac Source Ports for the signed macOS builds, akacross for tireless playtesting and pull requests, and everyone who reported issues after 0.14.0.
