title: Tim Peters has died
body_text: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 - Core Development - Discussions on Python.org = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Discussions on Python.org In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 Core Development guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python ( PEP 20 ), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float , because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink> ) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort : a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido 202 Likes guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:41am 2 Feel free to respond with your own Tim anecdotes. I could not cover everything he did. 9 Likes Rosuav (Chris Angelico) November 11, 2026, 6:04am 3 Very sad news. I have had the privilege and pleasure of discussing MANY topics with Tim, and his input into technical discussions has always been something I value very highly. He never treated you like an idiot, never dismissed your concerns out of hand, always answered and explained. I exchanged emails with him many times, but geography meant that sadly, we never met in person. 17 Likes hugovk (Hugo van Kemenade) November 11, 2026, 6:13am 4 Guido van Rossum: In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. From the start to the end. His last post concluded: Which is all a long-winded say of saying the real world is more complicated than our clean abstractions hope for . 48 Likes mcdonc (Chris McDonough) November 11, 2026, 6:41am 5 I wrote this some time ago about Tim: “”" I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career. Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido. Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them. Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either. It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt. Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot). When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered. Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim. He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so. Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start. Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim. When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on. It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it. “”" In sadness, . C 38 Likes duncathan (Dunc Graham) November 11, 2026, 6:46am 6 As a young child, only about 15, I first learned timsort. Some dozen years later, I had the briefest opportunity to exchange words with Tim himself on this forum. What a treat to have had that chance, just in time. RIP 11 Likes encukou (Petr Viktorin) November 11, 2026, 8:32am 7 When I was finishing university, head full of textbook algorithms, I read Objects/listsort.txt and was overwhelmed by how much depth, rigor, common sense and humanity can fit in a technical note. That was when I picked a programming language. 27 Likes pitrou (Antoine Pitrou) November 11, 2026, 9:53am 8 Tim’s main legacy for me has been the Zen of Python, which - despite being less cited nowadays - has been so useful and influential as a framework for elegance and clarity, and has informed so many people in their daily practice (and I cannot find a better way to describe him than as an excellent practitioner ). He was already less active when I started contributing around 2007; in fact my most frequent interactions with him have been in the recent years while he grew a slightly more confrontational attitude in some discussions, including here on d.p.o. I believe [1] he was acting with the best of intentions and was still deeply caring for the community he had been such a pivotal member of; acting with the same objectives as others, but having trouble to understand that different means might be used towards the same ends. and I might be full of myself here ↩︎ 18 Likes malemburg (Marc-André Lemburg) November 11, 2026, 9:58am 9 This is so sad and such a big loss for Python. Tim has given us a lot and we owe him. He was one of the extremely smart people who drew me into PythonLand in the late 1990s. Coming out of university, I was amazed how approachable, down to earth and humurous really great folks can be. Rest in Peace, Tim, and thanks-for-being-one-of-those-great-people-ly, Marc 19 Likes pf_moore (Paul Moore) November 11, 2026, 10:51am 10 So sad. I never had the chance to meet Tim in person, but his posts were always a delight to read, full of knowledge, insight and humour. I learned more than I can express from him. He will be missed. 14 Likes hodgestar (Simon Cross) November 11, 2026, 10:55am 11 One of the great souls, and roughly treated here near the end. 15 Likes nas (Neil Schemenauer) November 11, 2026, 12:31pm 12 A +1 to what Chris wrote. Tim was always pragmatic, preferring simple solutions over complex ones. In the early days of syntax highlighting in text editors, like Emacs and Vim, I remember that Python’s triple-quoted strings were tricky to get right. They span multiple lines and opening and closing tokens are identical, so it’s easy to get out of sync. Doctests make things especially tricky. I was telling Tim about some techniques I was using in the Vim syntax file to make it work more reliably. I don’t recall the editor Tim used (some commercial program on Windows) but he explained how he did it in his editor. Open the syntax highlighting config window, for open string token, type three quotes, for close string, type three quotes, close config window. Job done. That tickled him. He primarily used Windows 95 or 98 at a time when many Python core devs used NT, Unix, or Linux. He said if you installed all of Microsoft’s updates, it was quite reliable. Maybe he preferred it because it worked for him and there was no reason to change. Or, he found it useful when supporting people, since Windows was the most common platform Python was used on. Tim was about the furthest thing from an elitist you could be. This Bible quote comes to mind for me: “Ye shall know them by their fruits.”. Tim gave us a lot of fruit. I poked around at Python 2.4, since that seems a good version to show off the things he worked on. His contributions were all over the codebase but I’ll point out a few that stand out to me. pymalloc was contributed by Vladimir Marangozov but it was Tim who polished it to diamond-like form. A memory allocator is one of those things where it is impossible to have something completely optimal; you always make tradeoffs. Tim’s special contribution in that unit is Py_ADDRESS_IN_RANGE . It is well commented, if you want to understand how it works. Technically, it relies on undefined behavior but Tim figured it should work in practice. It did so for many years. At some point I wanted to increase the pymalloc pool size, since typical RAM sizes had increased so much since 2000. Tim helped me optimize the address_in_range() check. TimSort is a good example of Tim’s approach to software problems. Someone must have “nerd sniped” him on the problem of sorting. He already had an encyclopedic knowledge of the classic algorithms, like you’d find in Knuth. He spent a few days reading the recent research papers on sorting. With that knowledge and throwing in a few twists of his own, he made TimSort. He was always thinking of the common case, the favorable case as well as the worst-case scenarios. TimSort does all three well (it exploits already sorted runs, and uses galloping during merging to copy long stretches efficiently). Speaking of Knuth, the dict object algorithms were heavily optimized by Tim. The C file contains lots of comments. He also wrote dictnotes , which is a good example of his technical writing. Another example is weakref.txt , which I think Tim wrote after fixing a particularly difficult GC bug revealed by ZODB (while working at Zope Corp). On the topic of GC, the initial version of the cyclic garbage collector was written by me, merged before the 2.0 release. It was Tim who polished it into robust and well-performing shape. Likewise, I wrote the initial version of “simple generators” but it was Tim who put them on solid foundation, both the PEP and the implementation. Tim was skilled with numerical algorithms and error analysis, and Python benefited from his expertise. The float object and math module got special attention from him. He also worked on the Karatsuba multiplication algorithms in longobject . In addition to the C code, Tim also wrote beautiful Python code. As an example, see the N-Queens and Knight’s tour solvers in test_generators.py . He wrote the initial version of doctest . Some more examples of his work: difflib , pickletools , tabnanny (she shows no mercy!). It’s clear that Tim enjoyed writing code and solving problems. It’s also the case that he spent many thousands of hours of his time doing things primarily to help his fellow humans, without expectation of financial gain or of glory. Thank you, friend, for that and thank you for setting such an example. 40 Likes vinitkme (Vinit Kumar) November 11, 2026, 12:58pm 13 Thanks for everything Tim. Zen of Python has always been and will be my programming " North Star" and I strive to use it in every language I work with. Your impact has been on many of us Python Programmers and our families lives. Thank you and rest in peace! 8 Likes Stefan2 (Stefan Pochmann) November 11, 2026, 1:09pm 14 I’ve been fearing this since I noticed his absence end of July, dreading the thought whenever I saw his name but still no new activity. I’ve had quite a few interactions with Tim, he was one of my main contact points to Python, and he was the one who added me to Misc/ACKS . Thank you for everything, Tim. 7 Likes Paddy3118 (Paddy3118) November 11, 2026, 1:30pm 16 GNU Tim. 4 Likes diegor (Diego Russo) November 11, 2026, 2:39pm 17 I wish I’d had the chance to meet Tim in person. We had just a few exchanges on social media, but I always enjoyed reading his messages. There was always something to learn from his experience, his perspective and his way of thinking. Reading the memories shared here by those who knew and worked with him makes me regret even more that I never had that opportunity. I remember when Timsort was created. I was at university, studying algorithms, and it was a big deal at the time. But it’s the Zen of Python that influenced me most personally. “Now is better than never.” That sentence has stayed with me since I started using Python in the early 2000s. Over the years, it has become one of my personal mottos, encouraging me to keep trying, strive to do better and step outside my comfort zone, both in life and at work. We’ll probably never know what the 20th aphorism of the Zen of Python would have been. But perhaps that’s OK. I like to think that Tim left us the freedom to fill that space with something meaningful to each of us. Thank you, Tim, for everything you gave to Python and for the impact your work and words had on people. Rest in peace. 14 Likes holdenweb (Steve Holden) November 11, 2026, 3:09pm 18 Tim and I originally thought we first met fairly shortly after we both moved to Virginia, and became friends over Chinese lunches and discussions with Guido about starting a new Python conference. As we got to know each other better we realised that we had seen each other once before, when I visited a fellow academic’s office in Manchester, England, and Tim was there representing Cray Research back in 1983. Small world. After PythonLabs dissolved on Guido’s departure for the West coast the lunches eventually became a regular date at our local PF Chang, where Tim would invariably end with their huge “Mountain of Chocolate” dessert. The resulting sugar rush was often amusing. Tim was well-known long before I arrived in the Python world, and remained so after I left it. His technical contributions to Python, now the most popular programming language in the world, are legion. Just as significant, if not more so, was the way he communicated the joy, both of being a programmer and a human being. He was deeply affected by the ban imposed on him for ideological reasons by the Python Steering Committee but did not let that affect his desire to help others, which was on display until the end. I respected Tim above anyone else in the Python world for his wisdom, his witty humour and his deep humanity. There won’t be another one like him. Goodbye, old friend. 25 Likes sdeibel (Stephan Deibel) November 11, 2026, 3:41pm 19 This is very sad. I worked with Tim for quite a few years in context of the PSF board and of course also knew him from IPC and PyCons, starting in the relatively early days. He stood out to me almost immediately because so obviously utterly brilliant and yet with such a kind, helpful, respectful, good-humored way about him. One of the best people I’ve known, he was an inspiration to me and I think clearly also to very many others. Thanks, Tim, you will be missed. 8 Likes mwichmann (Mats Wichmann) November 11, 2026, 3:42pm 20 I only met Tim once, along with Guido, in 2001. I was writing a Python training course, and the training company wanted to arrange for “the experts” to get a look at it, so on a week I was in Reston working on it, we sat down over a meal. It wasn’t a very good course (“if I knew then what I know now”, a quarter century later…), but they generously gave of their time to critique, including Tim’s trademark humor, and I so appreciated it. He will be missed! 7 Likes mdickinson (Mark Dickinson) November 11, 2026, 4:00pm 22 Tim was hugely influential on my own CPython core development journey. Initially that influence was through his voluminous writings, mailing list discussions and his code itself: when I joined the core dev team in 2008, Tim himself was absent from the scene in person, but very much present through his many many contributions. Later on, after his return to core development, I was privileged to interact more directly with Tim on many topics. His gentle erudition, his humour and his patience were endless. Rest in peace, Tim. You will be sorely missed. 16 Likes next page → Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

dependency tree on a dedicated VT 2026-10-11 15:54:28 +02:00 README.md bootvine A live tree of systemd jobs on the boot console, in the spirit of nix-output-monitor . It replaces the scrolling kernel and systemd lines with the units still pending and, in the room the tree leaves, a timeline of the slowest ones that ran. I started bootvine out of frustration with the boot screen of most Linux distributions: a wall of log lines scrolling past too fast to read, which never gave me any idea of what was going on. It also follows shutdowns, answers passphrase prompts such as a LUKS unlock in place, and shows why a unit failed with its last journal lines. The guide walks through each part of the screen. Requirements systemd ≥ 246 as PID 1 libdbus and libsystemd a virtual terminal a systemd initrd, to show the boot from the initrd as well as stage 2 See Install for each distribution. Try it without installing With Nix , boot a sample NixOS machine with slow and failing units in a QEMU window, without touching your system's boot: nix run git+https://codeberg.org/wvhulle/bootvine#sample-vm-slow-services It logs in as root; poweroff shows the shutdown. The guide lists the other sample machines and the scripted demos that play in a terminal. Documentation Guide to the screen: the tree, the timeline, failures, shutdown and passphrase prompts. Install on NixOS, Ubuntu and other distributions. Configuration of colours, timing and the console. Architecture : how bootvine follows the boot and takes the console. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead. AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator . Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide Quick start With an AI coding agent Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent . aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1 Server mode (CLI and any SDK) Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator . See Getting started on Linux . Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker . Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator . Embedded mode (Rust tests) Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode , and Building from source below for its build cost. Known issues To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page . To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator . Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/ , and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/ . Building from source You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start ). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) ; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above. Prerequisites A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup ). A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code. At least 100 GB of free disk for target/ . The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added. A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster. Build and run cargo build -p aws-emulator-router cargo run -p aws-emulator-router The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate). Embedded mode build cost Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change. Repository layout . ├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates ├── services/ │ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE │ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol │ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal overrides │ │ ├── state.rs # this service's in-memory state │ │ └── ops/ # one file per operation │ └── tests/ ├── core/ │ ├── router/ # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint │ └── embedded/ # the in-process (embedded mode) facade ├── vendor/ # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update) └── issues/ # tracked fidelity issues Telemetry AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties. For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator . To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options. Use a command-line option Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t ) set to off . This setting applies only to that emulator process. aws-emulator --telemetry off In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command. Use an environment variable Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell. EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on , true , or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off , false , or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning. export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off aws-emulator Use a configuration file To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml . The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path. [ telemetry ] enabled = false Use the embedded configuration API In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator. use aws_emulator_embedded :: { AwsEmulatorEmbedded , EmbeddedOptions , Telemetry } ; fn main ( ) { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded :: new ( EmbeddedOptions :: default ( ) . telemetry ( Telemetry :: Off ) ) ; let _http_client = emulator . http_client ( ) ; } You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off. Reporting issues and contributing Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues . The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs. title: 93% of paint splatters are valid Perl programs (2019)
body_text: 93% of Paint Splatters are Valid Perl Programs | Colin McMillen Colin McMillen 93% of Paint Splatters are Valid Perl Programs Posted 2019-04-01. TLDR: read the paper and view the gallery of pretty Perl programs . In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl? We answer this question in the affirmative: it is possible to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs. Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. Winner of a Unwitting Participation Ribbon, “an unwelcome brand weâve affixed to each paper determined after careful scrutiny to have included a genuine artifact, thereby furthering the admirable causes of open science and fruitful procrastination.” Read it on Google Docs or download a PDF . Or grab the entire SIGBOVIK 2019 proceedings ; I’m on page 174. Supplementary Materials Here’s all the paint splatters on a single page, along with the valid Perl source code corresponding to each. “Not valid” is written in red for those images which did not parse as valid Perl programs. If different OCR settings recognized multiple valid Perl programs, I chose the one that seemed the most “interesting”, according to my own aesthetic sense. Here’s a tarball of 100 paint-splatter images that were used as the main dataset for this paper. (source code not available yet because i am bad at GitHub) Errata There are a few paint splatter Perl programs that I didn’t recognize as “interesting” until after the SIGBOVIK submission deadline. For example, this splatter is recognized by OCR as the string lerzfijglpFiji-j , which evaluates to the number 0 in Perl: The image below is recognized as the string -*? , which also evaluates to the number 0 in Perl: Another surprising program is shown below; OCR recognizes this image as the string ;i;c;;#\\?z{;?;;fn':.; , which evaluates to the string c in Perl: Finally, this image is recognized as the string ;E,'__' , which evaluates to the string E__ in Perl: © 2023 Colin McMillen . No cookies, no tracking.

body_text: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy - 9to5Mac Skip to main content Toggle main menu 9to5Mac Logo Go to the 9to5Mac home page Switch site 9to5Toys 9to5Google Logo 9to5Google Electrek Drone DJ Logo DroneDJ Space Explored About Privacy Toggle social menu Toggle dark mode Search for: Submit Toggle search form Forums Store Podcasts Apple@Work Happy Hour 9to5Mac Daily Overtime iPhone iPhone Mac Mac MacBook Pro MacBook Air iMac Mac mini Mac Studio Mac Pro iPad iPad Pro iPad Air iPad mini iPad iPadOS Watch Apple Watch Apple Watch Ultra Apple Health Apple Watch SE Vision Vision Pro visionOS Music and TV Apple Music AirPods HomePod Apple TV Guides Reviews How Tos AAPL Apple Store Apple Arcade Apple Card Apple Silicon Apple One Apple Fitness+ CarPlay Siri HomeKit Toggle dark mode AI Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy Ryan Christoffel  | Nov 10 2026 - 11:15 am PT 0 Comments Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’ The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more. It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details: Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf — Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026 As the post notes, here’s what the app does: Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone. And here are the feature highlights: Setup in minutes, not hours : “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.” Download and run models directly : “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.” Cluster for scale : “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.” Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead. Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments. title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server
body_text: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know | Wiz Blog Wiz Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Customers Company Sign in Under attack? Get a demo Blog Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know Detect and mitigate CVE-2026-119618, a critical RCE vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server. According to Wiz data, 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618. Immediate patching is advised. Merav Bar November 11, 2026 | A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE). As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. What is CVE-2026-119618? CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team. Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process. Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments? In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints. According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account. Which products are affected? The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below: Vendor Product Affected Versions Patched Versions Apache Software Foundation Apache HTTP Server From 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 2.4.71 and newer GitHub (Open Source) mod_h2 module From 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 2.0.42 and newer Which actions should security teams take? Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps: 1. Upgrade Deployments Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers() . Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42 . 2. Implement Temporary Mitigations If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector. Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf ) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references: # Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1 Protocols http/1.1 Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
body_text: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG - Apple Machine Learning Research Machine Learning Research Open Menu Close Menu Overview Research Highlights Publications Events Work with us content type highlight published November 5, 2026 Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution â a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs â rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs â is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently. In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions , a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) â once, offline, for a fixed database of keys â that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs. The Basics of Maximum Inner Product Search A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters â k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n â keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n / k â a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below. Figure 1: Geometric approaches to search can fail and miss nearest neighbors. This is due to their reliance on partitioning the space based on distances to centroids. In the animation, a nearest neighbor is missed as it is not associated with the nearest centroid. MIPS as a Support Function What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs) . Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself. The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input. Two Ways to Learn Maximum Inner Product Search If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best: The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality. KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Eulerâs theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced. Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter. Learned Routing with SupportNet As shown in Figure 1 , the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each clusterâs centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match. If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2 , in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings. Figure 2: Relying on distances to centroids can be misleading as those distances do not account for every key in each cluster. Given access to each clusterâs support function, assignment can be made based on how well a given query matches any key in a cluster. Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: âHow good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?â SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values. Figure 3: SupportNets approximate the support functions of each cluster and assign queries to clusters based on the best match with any key, not only centroids as typical geometric approaches do. We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup. Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top- s clusters matched with the query, where s grows as powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, â¦, 128) . Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters. The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9Ã faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids. The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90â93% of the time â up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) â versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline. SupportNet Router Size Family Latency (ms/query) Fraction of database scanned Figure 4: Routing performance (recall) due to SupportNets of various sizes versus latency or the fraction of the database we allow the router to scan. Routers, all with a depth of 16 layers, are trained on a 128-cluster Natural Questions dataset. SupportNets dominate the centroid router: given a latency target, one can get a higher recall with a SupportNet or conversely, that recall can be achieved at lower latency by a SupportNet than by a centroid router. Plugging Into Existing Indices SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a âquery rewriterâ in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5 : sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association. Figure 5: KeyNets are trained to map a query to its best match in a database. Combined with an IVF index, pre-processing queries via such a mapping makes search much easier: the resulting transformed query is now much closer to the target it is intended to retrieve. We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recallâcost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8Ã less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in âqualityâ provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89â97% of the time â up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) â versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11Ã fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it. KeyNet Searcher Size Family Latency (ms/query) Fraction of database scanned Figure 6: Search performance (recall) using an IVF index to search a database made from the Natural Questions dataset. The plots compare results due to querying the IVF index directly with raw queries against a search executed after mapping queries with KeyNets of various sizes, all with a fixed depth of 16 layers. Latency in the plots corresponds to the total time required to map a query and search, except for the raw-query case, which accounts only for search. Pre-processing queries with KeyNet is worth it no matter the size: the pre-processing overhead is compensated for by faster search downstream. We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNetâs predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep. Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query. Gallery item 1 Gallery item 2 Gallery item 3 Gallery item 4 Gallery item 5 Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'What is Matchbox Twenty?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'Who wrote The Eye of the World?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'What is a wind controller used for?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'When will the Summertime Ball be on?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'When was the show Victorious on Nickelodeon?' Which Network Should You Use? The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use KeyNet when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use SupportNet when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes â a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster. A New Direction for Learned Retrieval Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance â a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called amortization ) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve. Related readings and updates. Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions July 2, 2026 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICML Maximum inner product search (MIPS) is a crucial subroutine in machine learning, requiring the identification of a vector taken within a database (the keys) that best aligns with a given query. We propose amortized MIPS: a regression-based approach that trains neural networks to directly predict MIPS solutions, amortizing the cost of repeatedly solving MIPS for queries drawn from a known distribution over a fixed key database. Our key insight isâ¦ Read more Scalable Private Search with Wally October 16, 2024 research area Privacy This paper presents Wally, a private search system that supports efficient semantic and keyword search queries against large databases. When sufficiently many clients are making queries, Wallyâs performance is significantly better than previous systems. In previous private search systems, for each client query, the server must perform at least one expensive cryptographic operation per database entry. As a result, performance degradedâ¦ Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning. Our research in machine learning breaks new ground every day. Download for Mac · Windows · Linux Yogurt records your calls without adding a bot to the meeting. macOS 14.4+ (Apple Silicon) · Windows 10 2004+ (x64) · Ubuntu 22.04+ or similar (x64 AppImage) · 8 GB memory yogurt.so · Help · Build and run locally · MIT license Made by Frigade . What it does Live transcripts. Yogurt records calls and turns speech into text as you talk. Meeting summaries. Yogurt writes up the conversation and any notes you add. Private by default. Your audio, transcripts and AI processing stay on your computer. Free and open source. You can use Yogurt without an account. Who said what. Yogurt names speakers from Zoom, Teams and Meet on Mac only. Languages. Multi-language mode transcribes 99 languages. Recording reminders. Yogurt offers to record when a supported call starts. Answers with sources. Yogurt answers questions across meetings and links to the source. Folders and search. You can find meetings by folder, title, notes or transcript. Copy and export. You can copy notes or transcripts, or save both as Markdown. Local MCP server. Your chosen assistant app can read your notes when you allow access. Automatic stop. Yogurt stops recording when the call ends. Watch the demo yogurt-demo.mp4 How it works Record. Start recording your microphone and call audio; you can add your own notes. Transcribe. Yogurt uses whisper.cpp and, on supported Macs, Apple SpeechAnalyzer. Summarize and ask. A local open-weight model runs through llama.cpp. Meeting data stays local; Yogurt goes online for model downloads and update checks. Where your meetings, recordings, settings and models are stored Mac uses ~/Library/Application Support/Yogurt . Windows uses %APPDATA%\Yogurt . Linux uses ~/.config/Yogurt , or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Yogurt if set. FAQ What kind of computer do I need? A Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 14.4 or newer, a 64-bit PC with Windows 10 (version 2004) or newer, or a 64-bit Linux computer with Ubuntu 22.04 or newer. Each needs at least 8 GB of memory. If your computer is too slow, Yogurt tells you during setup. Calendar and speaker names from calls are Mac only for now. Windows says “Windows protected your PC.” What do I do? Click More info, then Run anyway. Windows shows this for new apps that aren’t signed with a Microsoft certificate yet. Yogurt is open source, so anyone can check what it does. Does Yogurt join my meetings? No. Yogurt records your microphone and the sound playing on your computer. No bot joins the call, so let the other people on the call know you’re recording. Are recordings saved? Yes. Your recordings, transcripts, and notes are saved locally on your computer. Is Yogurt free? Yes. Yogurt is free and open source under the MIT license. No account is needed. Does Yogurt work offline? Yes. After a one-time download of the AI models, transcription and summaries run locally on your computer. How much does setup download? It depends on your computer. Yogurt downloads a smaller notes model first, about 5 GB, then the best one your computer can run well, which can be 14 GB or more. Recording works once setup finishes, and notes and questions work offline once the notes model is in. How do I connect my assistant app? In Settings → AI apps , turn on access, copy the helper command, and add it as a local MCP server in your assistant app. Access is off by default. The app can read your meetings, notes and transcripts, but cannot change them. It may send what it reads to its own online model. Turn access off in Yogurt to stop further reads. Can other apps read my notes through MCP? Access is off until you enable it in Settings → AI apps . Apps get read-only access to meetings, notes and transcripts. Mac and Linux use a socket in your profile folder with 0600 permissions, so only your user account can open it. Windows uses a named pipe with a new random name each launch, stored only in your profile folder. There is no per-app token, so any app running under your account can read while access is on. Settings shows connected apps by their self-reported names. Which AI models does Yogurt use? Transcription uses Whisper through whisper.cpp, with large-v3-turbo or a smaller model depending on your computer. On supported Macs, Apple SpeechAnalyzer supplies live words while Whisper produces the saved transcript. Summaries and answers use a local open-weight model from the Gemma 4, gpt-oss or Qwen3 families, chosen for your hardware and run through llama.cpp. The app uses Electron and needs no account. Which languages does Yogurt support? Pick Multi-language in Settings → Language → Spoken language to transcribe 99 languages. You can also switch from the English menu in a note’s footer before or during recording. English only is the default. Summaries follow the meeting’s main language; answers follow your question’s language. Settings also offers 32 app languages. Which call apps does Yogurt work with? You can record calls in any app because Yogurt captures your microphone and system audio. Call detection covers Zoom, Teams and Meet. On Mac, Yogurt can also read their speaker names with Accessibility permission, when the call app shows who is speaking. How does Yogurt know a call has started? It checks which apps are using your microphone. For browser calls, it also checks the tab title or a nearby calendar event with a call link. This triggers an offer to record; recording starts only when you choose to. How do I connect my calendar? On Mac, allow Calendar access in Settings. Yogurt reads the calendars already on your computer and lets you choose which ones to show. You do not sign into a calendar account in Yogurt. title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
body_text: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine Home Blog Forum Sign in Subscribe Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex Ellie Huxtable 27 Oct 2026 — 4 min read Share Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run atuin resume 0:00 / 0:13 1× Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me. These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev , a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on. It’s a familiar problem! I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of .bash_history . But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds. Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things. Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily. Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work. Atuin Threads That is why we built Atuin Threads. Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop. Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this. Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own , or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too. Run atuin resume , and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post! It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever. Right now, we support Claude Code Codex Pi Omp OpenCode with more agents coming soon. MCP With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context. Our MCP is available as atuin mcp , and can be automatically installed with atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples: Work that never shipped I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better. These sessions contain the code that never made it into main , as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec. Object store outage With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬 My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with seeing some tigris avatar issues? led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch. Forking threads across machines Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups. One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm. I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too. Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work. Teams While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team. So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch? We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch ! While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep. Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+ Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh Run atuin resume to get started Use the MCP with atuin mcp install Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback! GitHub Forum Discord Read more Making Atuin sync 32x faster with packfiles Atuin sync is now 32x faster. We sync many thousands of records in single-digit seconds. 25 Aug 2026 Open Sourcing the Atuin AI Server Self host your own server for Atuin AI - the agent that lives in your terminal, and knows how you work 14 Jul 2026 Atuin v18.13 – better search, a PTY proxy, and AI for your shell A new release is out! v18.13 is probably the biggest set of changes we have released in a good while, read on to find out more. Much faster and better search with the daemon The daemon has existed for a long time, and has been marked as "experimental& 18 Mar 2026 Custom Keybindings for the Atuin TUI One of the longest-standing feature requests for Atuin has finally landed: full custom keybinding support for the search TUI. No more being stuck with our defaults, no more wishing ctrl-d did something else. Your TUI, your rules. 16 Feb 2026 Atuin Updates and news about Atuin, the magical shell tool Subscribe Email sent Powered by Ghost

Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio . The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed. Strong performance and calibration On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error. Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API. Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost. You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer: noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria. choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate. score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities. The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API . Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request: from google import genai client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"}) result = client.decisions.create( model="gemini-decision-1", input=[{ "type": "image", "uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg", "mime_type": "image/jpeg", }, { "type": "text", "text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.", }, ], questions={ "has_spill": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?", }, "next_action": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?", "criteria": { "wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.", "dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.", "ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.", }, }, "severity": { "type": "score", "instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.", "criteria": [ "Clean and ready.", "Minor localized spill.", "Major spill or safety hazard.", ], }, }, ) How teams are building with the Decisions API Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls: Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks. Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new rapid canvas experiment in Stitch uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish. Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency. Safety layer for MCP tools in Search : Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope. Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed). Start building today Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs. You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio , trying our Doorstep Parcels , Speed Sketch , and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation . Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel , LiteLLM , Pydantic AI , Pipecat , LiveKit , and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud.
