title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
body_text: How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Streetâs only NYC datacenter | Michael Bacarella Michael Bacarella _ Posts of varying effort on technology, cybersecurity, transhumanism, rationalism, self-improvement, DIY, and other stereotypical technologist stuff. How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter jane street war stories datacenter Published on 10 Nov 2026 by mbacarella A war story from Jane Street's systems team: a false smoke alarm, a datacenter with no cooling, and a sprint to pull every power cord before the sprinklers went off AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect. Everyoneâs heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didnât do titles, and we on the systems team werenât above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firmâs blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street. For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feelâ¦ odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didnât want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables. Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didnât exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner whoâd served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you donât trust the automation unless thereâs a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off. As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza , which was otherwise just a normal office building. When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. Iâd gone to a magnet high school in the city, so Iâd been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it. Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided Iâd get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called âpanty droppersâ, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stoneâs throw away in case there was an emergency. And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off. We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality theyâre not quite that dumb, but itâs close. Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually arenât kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads donât have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and thatâs when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they donât spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasnât been brought under control since itâs gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water. Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. Weâre still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, thereâs no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldnât spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!) Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands. And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything. I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands. Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet Iâd never heard before set in on the machine room. The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers. Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning. There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but thatâs a story for another day. As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time. But an across the board increase in temperature on many servers means thereâs a generalized cooling failure. What we needed was a system monitor built for this exact purpose, one we could trust to be ultimately, unfailingly reliable at the task of asking each Linux server for its temperature and computing a simple mean. Bash wouldnât cut it for this. Nor would Perl. No, a job of this magnitude called for the most reliable and type-safe programming language imaginable. So I fired up emacs and wrote it in good old OCaml: every minute, ask every server in each location directly for the temperature from its onboard sensors, take the average, and if itâs elevated, blast an alert out to everyone on the systems team to check for datacenter overheat. Yes, we could have also alerted if the CRAC units shut down or if a dedicated temperature sensor in the room was high, but the telemetry for this stuff was nowhere near as reliable, and unknown unknowns can still ruin you, so the most durable thing sometimes really is to ask your fleet of Linux boxes for their temperature and freak out if the average is just a little too high. Our team didnât interact much with the partner with the nuclear sub experience, but Iâd like to think he would have approved. Got a better tale of woe? body_text: We need more goat sacrifices - by Adam Mastroianni Experimental History Subscribe Sign in We need more goat sacrifices OR: OJ A-OK Adam Mastroianni Nov 10, 2026 275 81 36 Share Article voiceover 0:00 -24:35 Audio playback is not supported on your browser. Please upgrade. photo cred: my dad Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD , I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here . This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that. I won’t spoil the surprise, but I will say that a) it’s very silly, and b) I can’t wait to get mine. (For the US: US Residents, 18+. Ends December 11, 2026. See terms at https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder ) Anyway, onto the post! Before anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang. The point of this ritual is not to signal our obeisance to the gods (although if any of them want to stop by and help us out, that would be cool), but to remind ourselves that we know nothing. This is procedurally-induced humility, which is desperately necessary, because an alarming number of our best-intentioned interventions do not work . For example: In 2009, Congress spent $3 billion on “School Improvement Grants” for the worst-performing schools in the country. As far as we can tell, those grants did nothing . Universities that hired a Chief Diversity Officer between 2001 and 2019 did not end up with more diverse students, faculties, or administrators . The American government spent $280 million to help Afghan women get jobs, and now they can’t really say whether any women got any jobs . 1 Remember 20 years ago, when giving laptops to kids in developing countries seemed like the most important thing to do? Well, a 10-year RCT of 531 rural schools in Peru found zero effects of “One Laptop Per Child” on academic performance . 2 Researchers developed four different messages that were supposed to convince parents to vaccinate their kids. None of the messages worked, and one of them accidentally made parents more likely to believe that vaccines cause autism . Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures: When Arkansas added a work requirement to Medicaid, the number of Arkansans with health insurance went down without any increase in employment . In 2002, the Bush administration launched the Building Strong Families Program, which provided counseling to low-income, unmarried parents with the goal of strengthening their relationships, keeping them both in their child’s life, and ultimately getting them married. Three years later, an independent evaluation found that the program did none of those things . And here is the effect of four different abstinence-only sex ed programs that run across the United States: In the social sciences, nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassing . We can’t say that it’s impossible for anything like these programs to ever succeed, given enough time, flimsy theorizing, and generous definitions of “success”. The point is that these effects should be large, and instead they are nonexistent. Seems to me like it’s time to get the goats in here. HEAVY METAL It’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed? We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it. In 1987, the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a tongue-in-cheek paper that accidentally became his intellectual legacy. He would later refer to it as “far from being one of my favorites” and “the source of considerable embarrassment”, and yet it’s the only thing of his that I’ve ever read or even heard of. 3 It was called “ The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic Rules “, and it went like this, lightly paraphrased: The Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero. The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects. The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero. The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail. Rossi tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006 , insisting that there is now a “large number of well conducted impact assessments that yield statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”. Still, even after supposedly enduring 16 years of embarrassment from his one satirical paper, he concluded, “we really do not know whether programs over a wide variety of substantive areas are worth anything”. Rossi did not do us the favor of actually naming any of those “statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”, and I know why, because I have gone looking for them, and they are not easy to find. The Earned Income Tax Credit, which is designed to benefit low- and middle-income families, was once considered a slam dunk; now a new analysis suggests that it might not do anything . Plain packaging—where you strip cigarette boxes of their attractive branding—seems like a no brainer, but in Australia, it looks like the policy caused smokers to switch to cheaper brands and to smoke more . There’s a reading and math program that has done well in India , but as soon as other researchers tried to implement it elsewhere, the effects shrank . You can always find a one-off study showing that an intervention works, but if we’ve learned anything from the past 20 years of social science, it’s that one-off studies ain’t worth much. It’s so easy to juice your stats and journals are so hungry for positive results that entire literatures can be suspect, and decades of research can culminate in a shrug. “Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t, it depends on all sorts of factors that we can’t really specify, so uh, good luck!” Even if we take Rossi at his word and there are as-yet-unnamed programs out there that are reliable and effective, the question still remains: why aren’t there more of them? Why do so many of our best-laid plans end up like this: OJ A-OK The answer lies, I think, in a 50-year-old study that is almost certainly false. One of my favorite genres of psychology experiment is called something like: “the study is probably bullshit but the effect is probably real”. At the top of that heap is The Illusion of Control , a classic from 1975 and a favorite of Psych 101 classes everywhere. Usually, this study gets summarized as “people value their lottery tickets more when you let them pick the numbers vs. when you pick the numbers for them.” It’s as if people think that the mere act of picking imbues their ticket with a bit of juju, which makes them less willing to part with it. That would be a beautiful study, but it wasn’t the study that was actually conducted. The “lottery tickets” in question were in fact football cards, each one with a picture of a player, their team, etc. Some participants were given the opportunity to choose their football card and some had a card handed to them. Later, just before the drawing, all of the participants were asked how much it would take to buy their card back. On average, the pickers asked for $8.67, while the not-pickers said $1.86. 4 I’m sure you can see the obvious and less exciting explanation for these results: when people were given the chance, they picked their favorite players. The people who didn’t get to pick ended up with a card they liked less. This “illusion of control” effect is merely a “reality of people having preferences and acting on them” effect. 5 I wouldn’t let this one go either Unsurprisingly, well-powered, preregistered replications with actual lotteries have failed to find any difference in picking vs. not-picking . So that’s that: there’s no such thing as the illusion of control. Except... obviously there’s an illusion of control! Look around! People will blow on their dice at the craps table, they’ll don their lucky undies when the Knicks go to the finals, they’ll scream “look out!” to the hapless protagonists of a horror movie. When I was a kid, my parents used to send me off to play arcade games without any quarters, knowing that I would simply move the joystick in synchrony with the demo playing on the screen, convincing myself that I was causing the characters to move, when in fact I was merely mirroring them. Put it this way: why do you think The Secret has sold over 30 million copies ? It ain’t the beautiful prose or the sterling scientific evidence. It’s because when Rhonda Byrne tells you that “your thoughts are the primary cause of everything,” it feels kind of true. After all, can’t you jinx yourself by thinking the wrong thing? Haven’t you ever been like “whatever you do, don’t spill this soup” and then the next thing you know you’ve got a shirtful of bisque? And if brainwaves are powerful enough to spill soup, who knows what else they might do! So no, people don’t believe they can magically improve their chances of winning the lottery by picking the numbers themselves. Still, our intentions feel more potent than they should, and this shows up not only in our harmless superstitions, but also in the way we keep meddling in each other’s lives despite having no idea what we’re doing. 6 How do I know my preferred policies will have their intended results? Well, because I intend them. That’s not really my answer to the question; it’s the reason I don’t even think of the question in the first place. GEORGE W. BUSH, PROPHET OF OUR TIME Here’s the real evidence of our illusion of control: we’re so certain our interventions will work that we forget to check whether they do at all. For instance, the National Science Foundation funds over 1,000 STEM education projects, which are aimed at improving curricula, training, student outcomes, etc. According to an analysis by Stuart Buck , 76% of the time, the researchers running those programs don’t even attempt to evaluate them with actual experiments. Apparently if you have a bright idea about how to teach kindergarteners to code, you don’t need to bother assessing it. It turns out George W. Bush was actually right when he said : Speaking of the government, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office , many federal programs don’t even define their goals, let alone collect data on their progress toward those goals. For instance, the Department of Homeland Security is supposed to stop people from producing and distributing illicit fentanyl, and so they do things like search people’s cars and walk around with drug-sniffing dogs. When DHS was asked, “How do we know any of this is working? What would success even look like?”, they were like “hmm great questions”. They hadn’t set any goals or collected any data, despite being required to do so by law. As the GAO puts it with characteristic mildness: “As a result, DHS’s ability to fully understand the effectiveness of these efforts is limited.” Maybe it’s too much to expect that the Department of Homeland Security, especially in its current incarnation, would try to figure out whether it’s doing things that actually work. But it’s certainly not too much to expect of private philanthropists, who choose to give away their money of their own free will. Certainly they would care whether their dollars do anything. Right? Wrong. In 2018, Kenneth Langone, the Home Depot billionaire, donated $100 million to eliminate tuition fees at New York University’s main medical school. This was supposed to encourage med students to pick lower-paying specialties like pediatrics and primary care, and it was supposed to attract lower-income students to medical school in the first place. But neither of those things happened. The makeup of the student body hasn’t changed , and they’re picking the same specialities they always did. In this case, it should have been easy to foresee that those beaucoup bucks were going to do bupkis. First, medical school is already a good investment, regardless of income: yes, you take on a big pile of debt , but you also make a much bigger pile of money , even in the lowest-compensated specialties. Second, wiping out that debt does almost nothing to reduce the disparities between specialties: the average orthopedic surgeon earns $564,000 per year, while the average family practitioner earns about $281,000. If both of them work for 30 years, the surgeon earns about $17 million, while the family doc earns about $8 million. Meanwhile, the average medical school debt is about $200k , which is nothing compared to an extra $9 million over the course of your lifetime. And remember: in this situation, both the surgeon and the family doc attend for free, regardless of how much money they had when they arrived, or how much money they make after they leave. So there’s no reason why free tuition should encourage anybody to do anything differently—except to apply to NYU in the first place. And indeed, applications are up 47% . 7 To be clear, giving away dunderheaded donations is better than a lot of things that billionaires could be doing with their money, like buying a second superyacht or digging an additional doomsday bunker so they have a place to summer after the apocalypse. I’m glad that the plutocrats are trying to do something nice. I would just like them to succeed . THE GREAT BARRIER, GRIEF When people see our big heap of failed interventions, they tend to go through three stages of grief. Bargaining Okay, fine, these high-minded, utopian interventions don’t work, so what we really need is Common Sense and Obviously Good Ideas. For example, if you want to make poor people better off, you should give them money. That’s just Common Sense! That’s an Obviously Good Idea! Unfortunately, large, well-designed randomized controlled trials keep finding null effects of unconditional cash transfers . In one study , when low-income participants got $2000 with no strings attached, it made them less happy compared to people who got $500 or nothing at all. Psychologically, receiving 20 Benjamins was about 25% as bad as losing your job during the pandemic. That finding might be a fluke, but it also showed up in a study where researchers wiped out a bunch of people’s medical debt and it maybe made them more depressed . These programs do succeed in sense that when you give people more money, they have more money, and they spend it on things that they need. It’s just surprisingly difficult to find any evidence that having more money makes a difference. (Though note that results are more promising in low- and middle- income countries .) Denial This is where people typically raise the no true Scotsman defense: if we get bad results from a good idea, it must be because someone screwed something up, not because the good ideas were actually bad ideas. Maybe the measures were wrong, the implementation was shoddy, or the people who benefitted didn’t fill out the followup survey for some reason. This response isn’t totally irrational; programs go pear-shaped all the time. Maybe your One Laptop Per Child program only failed because all the laptops got stolen out of the back of the truck. Case in point: in that medical debt study, it seems like 76% of people didn’t even realize their medical debt had been wiped out. (But don’t get too excited: if anything, calling people and informing them of this boon made them slightly more depressed.) The real problem with no-true-Scotsman-ing these studies is that you must subscribe to the dubious belief that some tiny tweaks will somehow unlock giant effects. This is a holdover from pre-replication-crisis psychology, back when we thought you could, say, subliminally flash an American flag at someone and make them more likely to vote for a Republican two weeks later . It now seems like rinky-dink interventions tend to have rinky-dink effects, or none at all. So yes, we could always pick more appropriate measures, and the facilitators delivering the intervention could always have a bit more pep in their step. That might be enough to make a program slightly more effective, but it’s not enough to turn a null result into a blockbuster. Acceptance Acceptance sounds good, but it isn’t. Once we realize how hard it is to improve people’s lives, it’s tempting to believe that doing so is simply impossible, and so we are excused from even trying. This is a bit like finding out that bloodletting doesn’t work and then concluding that no medicine can ever work. (“Well, We’ve Tried Everything”, Says Society That Has Only Tried One or Two Things.) The social sciences are still in their alchemical stage. We do not understand the fundamental workings of the human mind , let alone what happens when those minds combine in societies and economies. Imagine trying to cure cancer using Galenic medicine or trying to land on the moon using Aristotelian physics—that’s what we’re doing when we roll out programs designed to change human behavior. FULL THROTTLE ARISTOTLE That doesn’t mean our ill-informed attempts can never succeed. Both Galen and Aristotle were right about some important things: it was Galen who figured out that urine is produced by the kidneys , rather than the bladder (as was commonly assumed), and it was Aristotle who successfully described how objects move in fluids , even if he attributed it to the wrong forces. But if we want to solve real, Hydra-headed problems, we need more than a handful of facts. (“Doc, I’m all itchy and covered in spots! What do I do?” “Hmm...did you know that urine is produced in the kidneys?”) Until psychology and its neighboring disciplines grow into scientific maturity , all we can do is guess and check. There’s nothing shameful in that, but there is something shameful in pretending otherwise. This is hard for us to internalize, because by default we assume that we were born near the end of history. We understand, of course, that we still have a few things to figure out, but emphasis on the few . Just look at our beautiful universities, our begowned scholars, our numerous and inscrutable papers! How can you say we know nothing when we have so many TED talks? We misunderstand what it feels like to be in the middle of things. Almost no one who read Galen or Aristotle ever thought to themselves, “oh, obviously this is only version 0.1 of our knowledge, all of this is tentative and incomplete, and one day it will be overturned and replaced with something better, something that actually works.” No, they thought to themselves, “Thank u Mr. Aristotle for your many true and useful facts.” 🙏 That’s why the worst possible reaction to a failed intervention is resignation . We may not know enough to improve our lot right now, but perhaps we could figure it out, if we tried. Maybe that means another RCT, or maybe it means another century of futzing around in the fundamentals before we can do anything useful. (This does put a ceiling on the utopia we can expect to achieve in the near future. If you believe that we can perfect human nature by reorganizing society to your specifications, you would do well to remember that, as of now, we can’t even get people to go to the gym .) That may seem unfair—what a bummer to be born in medias res , when so many of our problems remain unsolved! But if it is an affront, every human before us has been similarly affronted, and some of them chose to begin the work anyway. Whenever we pluck a low-hanging fruit today, it’s only because someone else planted a seed that they never got to harvest. So why should we expect to pluck without planting? As Seneca put it nearly 2,000 years ago : I revere the discoveries of wisdom and their discoverers [...] For me those things were acquired, for me they were labored for. [...] Let us make larger what we have received. Let this heritage pass from me to posterity increased. I know some people don’t feel this way. Some believe that the answers are simple and known and merely need to be enacted by force . Others think the answers are unknowable and will remain so forever . For those folks, I offer an invitation: the next time we conduct the ritual before undertaking some new policy, they may have the honor of playing the part of the goat. ( source ) Experimental History is produced in the kidneys Subscribe 1 Of course, that sum is negligible compared to $4-6 trillion we spent trying and failing to turn Afghanistan and Iraq into thriving democracies. 2 How times have changed: I know parents who spend hours commuting every day just so their kids can attend a school that won’t issue them a laptop. 3 Other times an academic made a joke that went on to become their most prominent work: In 2009, four neuroscientists published a poster —not even a paper!—showing that, with fMRI techniques that were standard at the time, it was possible to detect activity in the brain of a dead salmon. As far as I can tell, this is one of the most-cited publications, if not the most-cited publication, for every single author. Andre Geim won the Nobel Prize in 2010 for his work on graphene, but when people stop him at conferences they want to talk about that time he used diamagnetism to make a frog float . Stigler’s Law of Eponymy : “No scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer.” Named after Stephen Stigler (and by Stephen Stigler), originally discovered by Robert Merton. Cited more than most of Stiglers other papers. Goodhart’s Law was originally a “ jocular aside “ in a paper about monetary policy, and is now the claim for which he is best known. 4 $68.09 and $15.39 today, respectively. 5 There are five other studies in the paper that purport to show similar effects, but none of them inspire much confidence. Most of these studies have like 15 participants in each condition, which is not enough to detect big honking effects like “people have more lapses in attention when you deprive them of sleep for 24 hours” (required N = ~28 well-rested people, 28 sleep-deprived people). 6 In this way, I think the illusion of control may be another triple-decker fallacy, much like the one I described in Bamboozle Me, Daddy : There’s the illusion of control: people assume they have more influence over the course of events than they really do An illusion of the illusion of control: The original demonstrations of the illusion of control were probably flukes or fraud And an illusion of the illusion of the illusion of control: Nevertheless, people still seem to believe they have more influence of the course of events than they really do, and so if you believe there is no such thing as the illusion of control, you are probably subject to an illusion yourself 7 And after this resounding non-success, Langone donated another $200 million to also eliminate tuition at NYU’s separate Long Island School of Medicine . 275 81 36 Share Previous Discussion about this post Comments Restacks TW 2d Liked by Adam Mastroianni In terms of control, I'm thinking of Wiseman's studies on luck. (Not a scientist, have no idea about the math on the original papers, but it sounds compelling enough.) He found that some people are more lucky than other people, and nearly all lucky people consider themselves to be lucky. His thesis, based on a couple ingenious experiments, is that lucky people, for whatever reason, *notice things in their environment more readily*, most usually opportunities. Visualizing does seem to work, at least not to hurt, some people; perhaps it's a way of trying to train yourself to notice things differently. It certainly crops up with surprising regularity in the careers of authors you've heard of. Interestingly, *actual* medieval magic practitioners believed this is how magic really worked. It wasn't some kind of empirical or physics-based process as so many science folks assume. Reply Share 4 replies Vara La Fey 2d Liked by Adam Mastroianni Thought-provoking article. But the primary thought it provoked in me is that the "results" aren't checked because the actual intended result has already been achieved: successful transfer of money, power, or prestige. It seems to me that all of the failures you mention have that one successful result in common. And once that one successful result is achieved, there is little incentive to analyze the post-result trivia. Yes, I'm saying these interventions are grifts, but you analyzed them as if they were honest. Reply Share 1 reply by Adam Mastroianni 79 more comments... Top Latest Discussions Ready for more? title: Smart home devices should work without the internet
body_text: Smart home devices should work without the internet — Do Code That Matters Do Code That Matters Blog About Do Code That Matters Blog About Smart home devices should work without the internet Oct 2026 · 3748 words · 19 min read · Spencer Kittleson Your browser does not support the audio element. Download audio Scissors cutting an ethernet cable under the words No Internet, No Problem. AI;DR: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own. Secondary note: From HN, I know you don’t like AI written content so I’ve reworked most of this post to be written in my own words. The slide decks are the most interesting, LLMs were used to add context. I’m making those available as downloads for first talk and then second talk . TLDR; Every core smart device in my house does not depend on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, everything works (downgraded experience perhaps). It has been my rule for 10 years and it has been challenging to follow. I’ve given two talks about it. Check out each slide by slide. Why local My Nest integration worked one day until it didn’t. They had changed the api (around the same time Google acquired them). I have a few more examples in these talks that show a samsung fridge and a grill controller that needs wifi to show temperature. I don’t/shouldn’t need wifi and/or vendor service to interact with hardware. So everything that matters runs on hardware I own. Mostly on Tasmota on esp8266/esp32 boards, MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services for enhancements like Alexa and a few AWS ones BUT those are secondary. If the internet is down, the switches all work like normal. The rules From the first talk: No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. Be agile. Check your automations. Exceptions must be exceptional. Added after year five, once more people lived in the house: A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house. Configuration lives in one place instead of five vendor apps. More than one way to do something. An app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag. If I keep doing the same steps, it becomes routine (node red or on the tasmota device itself). Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point. No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. I get asked about the the Tasmota sprinkler controller the most as well as the garage door setup. Both have been running for years with no real changes. Talk One: Home Automation Nobody needs any of this. I like building things that just work in the background. Each automation is a small puzzle. Its a hobby. Everything seems to want to reach out to the cloud. Laptops, phones, etc make sense. However my thermostats and locks… smart devices need to be questioned since they could be critical useful in your home. They may go out of business so be mindful what your signing up. Many start start with these devices: thermostat, smart plug, smart lock. Each can have its own account and app. Usually people will try to combine devices into the same ecosystem when possible. Know this triangle: cloud cam is cheap and easy but in exchange for costs you privacy. A smart plug I flash myself takes longer to set up, but I can hook it into anything. Figure out where a device lands before buying it. This is bad behavior. Don’t tape switches to the on position. The better fix is an in-wall Wi-Fi switch. It still works like a normal switch and I can automate it. More work to install than a smart plug. Nobody has to change their habits. Rule one: if the internet goes down, my lights still turn on. Being agile means willing to understand that changes will come that you must in your system. A small workflow to keep my garage cool in the summer time. I’ve had to change it multiple times. I have a reed switch wired up to the tasmota esp32 that controls the garage door with global state. I use grafana to monitor the state changes. I want to know if the garage door was left open so i could get message to me that its been open for too long. Scheduled triggers on a single pump. Be careful here, automations fighting over one device can happen and has caused me problems. Make it a habit to check every so often. Broken many of these rules so now i refer to them as guidelines! Three ways to do “event in, action out.” Node-RED is my main tool. Alexa routines and IFTTT-style applets cover the stuff I don’t want to build myself. MQTT keeps things decoupled as a pub sub event system. The temperature sensor publishes and doesn’t care who’s listening. So a phone and a backend can both subscribe without the sensor doing anything extra. The sprinkler controller in the Tasmota post works the same way. A Sonoff Mini fits inside the fireplace wiring, and the dashboard or Alexa can flip it. A fake fire you can turn on by voice is a good party trick. The whole sprinkler build: the relay and ESP module in the enclosure, the 3D board render, the Tasmota UI with BME280 sensor readings, the Node-RED schedule feeding the pump, and the finished PCB layout. The sprinkler post has the full writeup, including why I picked Tasmota over custom firmware. It’s a bit hacky but I love it :D Talk one in five lines. The one I break most is the first, don’t introduce a new way while removing the old one, and I regret it every time. The last one stops me from breaking the others for no good reason. “I was in a hurry” doesn’t count. That was talk one. Most of the “memorable automations” later broke in some new way or got replaced, so there’s a sequel. Talk Two: Home Automation, The Sequel Enough time passed between the talks that I had a new list of problems. More devices means more decisions made without me. It’s a little unsettling but mostly harmless. Everyone else is dealing with this too from what I can see. The same rules from talk one (worded a bit tighter). The rules stayed the same but more were added. My setup assumed one person lived in the house. More people meant traffic pattern differences and additional access keys. Also, I would be longer away. So I needed two additional systems water flooding detection and presence detection. Same joke, new rules. These are rules 6 to 11 at the top of the post. Now the builds! A motor and PVC pipe rig for outdoor lighting, a UV grow light clipped to a houseplant, and a UV strip under the cabinets for sanitizing. Random automations with a water pump, AirGradient kit, and robot vacuum. This dashboard replaced more apps than anything else: garage door, side door unlock, front lock, all lights on or off, brightness, a coffee bar color picker, and warm-to-cool for the living room. It’s one cheap tablet next to the thermostat. No one needs an app. Its a physical device everyone can go to if needed. The lights behind the TV run through the same system instead of their own remote. These lights turn on when the TV comes on. Shuts off at smart times as well. I do recommend smart locks when you need to have access controls in places other than just keys. Check out the parts at the end of this post to see what I have used. The ESP32 D1 mini handles anything custom (it’s cheap). I’ve been able to find smart plugs I can flash with Tasmota. The Raspberry Pi 2 B runs Node-RED and Grafana. LED strips for ambient lighting, power transistors for higher-current loads, and small relay modules so a microcontroller can switch mains voltage safely. The rest of the bin: a resistor assortment, color-coded wire so I can trace a circuit later, and a capacitor kit for smoothing and timing. Node-RED for the logic, Grafana to see what’s happening, Tasmota on anything I flash, Telegram for notifications, and Python or JavaScript for glue code that doesn’t fit in a flow. My Garage flow today. It’s crazy but it works and gets changed often. This is the “is everything okay” dashboard: humidity, temperature, dew point, pressure and gas on one side, and energy use, door opens and on-status history on the other. I built it because I got tired of guessing. Dashboards and Grafana panels work for me. Everyone else in the house just wants the light on. The “more than one way in” rule in hardware: the wall tablet for whoever is standing there, NFC tags and a QR code to tap, and an Echo Dot for anyone who would rather talk to the house. The tools I build and debug all of this with. That’s both talks five years apart. The rules barely changed, just extended. The list of problems kept growing. A third talk is coming around agentic use cases. The same rules should hold when an AI agent is the one flipping the switches. I expect to add a few more rules in the process. What Readers are telling me I shared this post on LinkedIn and Hacker News and asked for the most pointless internet dependency people had found in a device. Summarizations of those thoughts: Everyone has one Most examples were basic functions locked behind an app, an account, or a server: A fridge whose temperature can’t be changed because of a bug in the manufacturer’s phone app. A TV that can’t even switch inputs when the internet is down, and another that has to be signed in before it works as a plain HDMI monitor. One reader’s older smart TV has dead apps but still works as a regular TV, which is how a device should fail. A heating system whose app doesn’t work from the local network. A kitchen vent and a dishwasher that need the internet even when you control them from Home Assistant. A smart plug that can’t be set up on an isolated network. Noise-cancelling headphones that search for a Bluetooth device forever, so you can’t just turn on the noise cancelling. Synthesizers and MIDI keyboards that need a cloud login for first use or firmware updates. A meat thermometer that only worked through its app and stopped working when the company went out of business. The meat thermometer bothers me most. The hardware outlived the company. It stopped working anyway. Rules readers added Offline first, with the internet for extras. A device should do its main job on its own. Treat every third-party dependency as a risk. APIs change, so plan a local fallback or a clear degraded mode. One mobile developer works the same way: the core action works offline or from cache, and only the extras wait for a connection. Decide what must work offline. My answer is turning things on and off, temperature and safety controls, and anything a guest has to use without learning an app. As one reader said, if a visitor can’t turn something on or adjust the temperature without an app account, the design has failed. A stricter version of my first two rules: everything core works with the Wi-Fi or the automation server shut down, and smart features never take away the dumb ones. The wall switch should control the light directly and let automation flip it. A switch that only sends a request to the automation fails. That reader says my sprinkler controller fails this bar too. The only sprinkler controller they’d found with a local API and full control on the device itself was RainMachine, which is gone. Clean up when you throw things away. Remove a connected printer from your account first. An abandoned connected device can be an easy way in for an attacker. Practical tips Use local protocols. One reader recommends Zigbee and Z-Wave over Wi-Fi, because a switch that doesn’t need the cloud tends to behave the same year after year. Another uses Zigbee for the smart plugs that can’t be set up without internet. Let an LLM find the firmware. One reader buys the cheapest hardware that does the job, ignores reviews that complain about the app, and asks an LLM for local-first custom firmware once it arrives. That has worked for their switches, a thermostat, an air quality monitor, a thermometer, and a window fan. They’d have paid about 2.5x for hardware that was local out of the box. Old Nest thermostats have a way out. No Longer Evil is open source firmware for Nest Gen 1 and Gen 2 thermostats. Smart TVs can be tamed. Reset the TV and never connect it to the network, and the input problem goes away. Remote access is the cost of staying local. I use Tailscale on the router and keep the individual devices off the tailnet. One reader ran OpenVPN on OpenWrt, which worked but felt clunky, and is now trying Tailscale. There’s a gap to fill. One reader would happily pay for a pre-built, open “works with everything” Raspberry Pi image with MQTT. DietPi and OpenWrt come close and have a small footprint, but you need some understanding to get going. Another wanted a hub that ships with the house, like a water heater or a router. Home Assistant sells hub hardware that’s close to that. Right to repair is the bigger fight. Readers pointed to the right-to-repair movement and groups like the FULU Foundation , which work to keep companies from locking you out of what you bought. Counterpoints Internet connectivity has real cases that are obvious, such as a meat thermometer that lets you watch the game while the steak cooks. Remote access to systems where you really need them such as cameras. Devices I’ve used (This section has Amazon affiliate links. If you buy through them, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) These are the parts from my home automation builds, grouped by project. Sprinkler controller Gear Purpose Buy HiLetgo ESP8266 NodeMCU board (3 pack) Wi-Fi microcontroller that runs Tasmota Amazon SSD1306 OLED screen Status display for the sprinkler state Amazon Inkbird SSR-40DA solid state relay Switches the 24 VAC sprinkler valve Amazon BME280 sensor Temperature, humidity and pressure Amazon 24 VAC power supply Powers the sprinkler valve Amazon Lights, switches and plugs Gear Purpose Buy Martin Jerry smart dimmer switch (Tasmota pre-flashed) Wall light switch that runs Tasmota out of the box Amazon Martin Jerry humidity fan switch Runs the bathroom fan when humidity gets too high Amazon Sonoff S31 smart plug Power watchdog for the cable modem Amazon Serial-to-USB adapter Connects an ESP8266 to your PC for flashing Tasmota Amazon Garage door Gear Purpose Buy Raspberry Pi 3 Runs Docker and the web API Amazon SunFounder 2-channel 5V relay module Simulates the button press to toggle the door Amazon LiftMaster wired control panel (78LM, replaces the 41A5273-1) Bypasses the anti-tamper wiring Amazon Around the house Gear Purpose Buy GL.iNet Flint 2 router (GL-MT6000) Runs OpenWrt and an MQTT broker locally Amazon Cheap tablet Mounted on the wall as the dashboard Amazon Lefant robot vacuum Cleans the floors Amazon See something inaccurate or need more detail? title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
body_text: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers - CBS News Latest U.S. Iran War Trump Interview Midterms World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds MoneyWatch | Managing Your Money CBS News Price Tracker Watch CBS News MoneyWatch United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers By Megan Cerullo Megan Cerullo Reporter, MoneyWatch Megan Cerullo is a New York-based reporter for CBS MoneyWatch covering small business, workplace, health care, consumer spending and personal finance topics. She regularly appears on CBS News 24/7 to discuss her reporting. Read Full Bio Megan Cerullo November 11, 2026 / 2:37 PM EST / MoneyWatch Add CBS News on Google United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing  security risks  and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules. Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases. To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles." The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances. "As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule. United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.  "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches." Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.  United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline." "But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.  Edited by Alain Sherter Kris Van Cleave contributed to this report. title: Lock Your GitHub Actions
body_text: Lock your GitHub Actions · Hugo van Kemenade ↓ Skip to main content Hugo van Kemenade Blog Tags Lock your GitHub Actions 11 November 2026 github-actions security gh Table of Contents Install Lock ’em Renovate and Dependabot Validate zizmor Locked! Examples GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles . Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code. For example, an old workflow looks like: name : Lint on : [ push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch] permissions : {} env : FORCE_COLOR : 1 RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT : github jobs : lint : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 with : persist-credentials : false - uses : j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0 Here’s how I set up lockfiles. Install # Install the gh-actions-lock extension to the gh CLI : $ gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock ✓ Installed extension github/gh-actions-lock Lock ’em # In your repo, run: $ gh actions-lock ✓ All 1 workflows valid The workflow now uses vX.Y.Z tags and looks like this: diff --git a/.github/workflows/lint.yml b/.github/workflows/lint.yml index 946971c..3503607 100644 --- a/.github/workflows/lint.yml +++ b/.github/workflows/lint.yml @@ -13,7 +13,7 @@ jobs: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 + - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1 with: persist-credentials: false - - uses: j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0 + - uses: j178/prek-action@v3.1.0 And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock : # This file is machine-generated by `gh actions-lock`. # Do not edit by hand; run `gh actions-lock` to update. # Docs: https://gh.io/actions-lockfile version : 'v0.0.3' workflows : '.github/workflows/lint.yml' : - 'actions/checkout@v7.0.1' - 'j178/prek-action@v3.1.0' dependencies : 'actions/checkout@v7.0.1' : ref : 'v7.0.1' commit : 'sha1-3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1' owner_id : 44036562 repo_id : 197814629 'j178/prek-action@v3.1.0' : ref : 'v3.1.0' commit : 'sha1-44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d' owner_id : 10510431 repo_id : 1052387486 Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile. Renovate and Dependabot # Good news, both already support lockfiles ! Your periodic updates will also update the lockfile. Remember to use cooldowns . Validate # GitHub also recommends verifying lockfiles in CI to ensure it’s up-to-date and not corrupt. They suggest copying this verify-lockfile.yml into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job so it runs independently and in parallel: name : Lint on : [ push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch] permissions : {} env : FORCE_COLOR : 1 RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT : github jobs : lint : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v7.0.1 with : persist-credentials : false - uses : j178/prek-action@v3.1.0 # Fails when .github/workflows/actions.lock is out of sync with the # workflows or a locked pin no longer verifies upstream. lockfile : runs-on : ubuntu-slim env : GH_TOKEN : ${{ github.token }} steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v7.0.1 with : persist-credentials : false - run : gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock --pin v0.4.1 - run : gh actions-lock --verify Note I’m using the lightweight ubuntu-slim runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1; we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for another time. Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with gh actions-lock . Nothing actually changes if adding to lint.yml because it’s already locking actions/checkout . But if you created a new file like verify-lockfile.yml , you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know. zizmor # zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and strongly recommended . If you don’t use it, please do. Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to support lockfiles. I use zizmor in prek , so add/update zizmor in .pre-commit-config.yaml : - repo : https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-pre-commit rev : v1.32.0 hooks : - id : zizmor Locked! # OK, commit and push! Examples # python-pillow/Pillow#10428 python/release-tools#477 python/miss-islington#758 python/cpython#161811 Header photo: Slaymaker Barry Co. Sprocket Locks in The Bearings (vol. XII no. 23, 2nd January 1896) in the Smithsonian Libraries and Archives , with no known copyright restrictions .
