Full OpenCL output .-----------------------------------------------------------------------------. |----------------.------------------------------------------------------------| | Device ID 0 | NVIDIA Graphics Device | | Device ID 1 | NVIDIA Graphics Device | |----------------'------------------------------------------------------------| |----------------.------------------------------------------------------------| | Device ID | 0 | | Device Name | NVIDIA Graphics Device | | Device Vendor | NVIDIA Corporation | | Device Driver | 610.43.03 (Linux) | | OpenCL Version | OpenCL C 3.0 | | Compute Units | 124 at 1410 MHz (7936 cores, 22.380 TFLOPs/s) | | Memory, Cache | 81338 MB VRAM, 3472 KB global / 48 KB local | | Buffer Limits | 20334 MB global, 64 KB constant | | Max Workgroup | 1024 threads | |----------------'------------------------------------------------------------| | Info: OpenCL C code successfully compiled. | | FP64 Compute (double, fma ) 11.287 TFLOPs/s (1/2 ) | | FP32 Compute (float , fma ) 22.781 TFLOPs/s ( 1x ) | | FP16 Compute (half2 , fma ) 85.858 TFLOPs/s ( 4x ) | | INT64 Compute (long , a*b+c) 2.759 TIOPs/s (1/8 ) | | INT32 Compute (int , a*b+c) 22.769 TIOPs/s ( 1x ) | | INT16 Compute (short2, a*b+c) 20.273 TIOPs/s ( 1x ) | | INT8 Compute (char4 , dp4a ) 81.169 TIOPs/s ( 4x ) | | Memory Bandwidth ( coalesced read ) 1883.17 GB/s | | Memory Bandwidth ( coalesced write) 2137.93 GB/s | | Memory Bandwidth (misaligned read ) 1460.81 GB/s | | Memory Bandwidth (misaligned write) 250.13 GB/s | | PCIe Bandwidth (send ) 13.10 GB/s | | PCIe Bandwidth ( receive ) 11.69 GB/s | | PCIe Bandwidth ( bidirectional) (Gen3 x16) 11.58 GB/s | |-----------------------------------------------------------------------------| '-----------------------------------------------------------------------------' NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIAâs design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses! In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. Iâve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here . Acknowledgements My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIAâs product security team ahead of the publication of this article. GA100 versions The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I wonât delve into every SKU , but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100. As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentationâundifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand. In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile. SKU Out-of-box Software (cmpunlocker) GA100VFI CMP 170HX 8GB Framebuffer 8 GB 64 GB 64-80 GB 1 CMP 170HX 10GB Framebuffer 10 GB 40 GB 2 40-48 GB Both CMPs SMs 70 70 120-128 PCIe generation 1 2 4 NVLink No No Yes 3 ECC No No Yes 4 Multi-Instance GPUs No No Yes 4 NVDEC 0 0 5 4 Hardware restrictions So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100. The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable âoption wordsâ to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled. Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions: Regular fuses (rows 0-221). These are straightforward; often single (pairs of) fuses will map to an option word, such as OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM (an option word that determines whether further fuse programming is allowed or not). Regular fuses have built-in redundancy: for example, OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM consists of a PRI and RED (primary and redundant) fuse, in this case the primary instance is fuse 0 of row 0, and the redundant is fuse 0 of row 1. Some option words are scalars, such as OPT_X_COORDINATE, which is 9 bits wide and ostensibly holds the x-coordinate of the die on the fabbed wafer. Importantly, if a regular fuse is blown, there is basically no remedy to persistently unblow it (save for RIR later). Fuseless fuses (rows 222-487). This is a weird one. Apparently NVIDIA got frustrated with accidentally blowing regular fuses and ruining their engineering samples, and came up with a system to encode effective option words in a JTAG chain-like format (see this patent ). Think about FF as essentially a script that describes what option words should have what values. FF fuses (excuse the RAS syndrome ) concern most of the functionality we can unlock using VFI. This is because FF option words can be trivially cleared by simply writing new FF rows! Weâll about this more in depth, later. For now, you should know that NVIDIA also knows this, because under normal conditions, you are strictly prevented from performing any FF fuse blows. IFF fuses (rows 487-512). These contain instructions in a different format than the FF one. Theyâre out of scope for this post, and theyâre mainly useful for on-the-fly reprogramming of fuse controller option words. They are usually not accessible in a production card. RIR fuses (8 rows of 32 fuses, which are technically not part of the 512 rows). These are provided by the designer of the fuse macro (TSMC datasheet here ) and are essentially the first party designerâs intended âfuse repairâ mechanism. The RIR section on a GA100 has space for 16 repair instructions, each overriding the value of an identified single fuse in the main 512 rows. Unfortunately for us, specifically in the 8 GB 170HX SKU, 15 of the 16 RIR words are all ones, and the 16th word encodes a useless repair instruction that can only be rarely leveraged for any interesting unlock. The story is different for the 10 GB SKU, but thatâs a matter for another dayâ¦ There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock: âControl fusesâ. The term comes from NVIDIAâs Tegra hardware headers, they use it to refer specifically to rows 0 and 1, which specify the values of highly security-sensitive option words. Fuseless fuses, which encode all of the interesting option words that decide whether a GA100 is born to be a measly mining card or an AI datacenter workhorse. Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, weâll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in. Fuseless fuses Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0â4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6â15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16â31 supply that blockâs new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words. If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, 0x0fe805c1 means chain 1, block 23, data 0x0fe8 . Appending that record can clear an effective bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1. Now that we know how FF words are encoded, hereâs a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping. Named option Inferred FF location Use NV_FUSE_OPT_FBIO_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 83â106; blocks 5â6 Memory I/O floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_FBPA_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 107â130; blocks 6â8 Memory subpartition floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_GPC_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 131â138; block 8 GPC floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC0_DISABLE through NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC7_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 187+8i through 194+8i for GPC i ; blocks 11â15 Eight TPC masks NV_FUSE_OPT_PES_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 251â274; blocks 15â17 PES floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_FBP_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 307â318; block 19 Framebuffer partition floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_ROP_L2_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 319â342; blocks 19â21 ROP/L2 floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 368â370; block 23 NVLink disable mask NV_FUSE_OPT_DISABLE_GEN3_SPEED Chain 2 block 39; which of bits 1 and 9 is unresolved PCIe Gen3 speed restriction NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_MAGIC_BITS_D[25] Chain 2 block 47 bit 3 Gen4 speed-disable flag NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN23_DISABLE Chain 2 block 49 bit 6 PCIe boot policy NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN3_DISABLE Chain 2 block 49 bit 7 PCIe boot policy NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_DEVIDA Chain 2, bits 593â608; blocks 37â38 Device identity NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_DEVIDB Chain 2, bits 609â624; blocks 38â39 Device identity NV_FUSE_OPT_SYS_PIPE_DISABLE Chain 1, bits 372â379; block 23 Multi-instance GPU enabled pipes The acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other: FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a âframebuffer partitionâ, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function. With this knowledge in hand, what if we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, weâll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being âfloorsweptâ. After illuminating the âwhat-ifâ, Iâll talk about the âhowâ: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI. Floorsweeping NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controllerâs effective status words for each functional block. Letâs take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852 : FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate OPT_FBP_DEFECTIVE mask was 0x840 , covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to 0x840 with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the dieâs 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852 , became responsive after this fuse write. Although the functional blocks can be âunfloorsweptâ with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example. To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlocker âs method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G. Achieving the FF burn With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Letâs take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more. To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow: The fuse controller has an internal FSM, and it indicates its current state via the FUSECTRL_STATE bits. The fuse controller enters a WRITE_PROGRAM state per each âhotâ bit in the requested FUSEWDATA value. This tracks with the expected fuse programming behavior. However, unless a specific option word is cleared, writes to fuse addresses outside of the FPF range (rows 96-221) do not actually take place. Fuses in this region (believed to be âfield programmable fusesâ indicating a watermark of which ucode versions have run, alongside other field-relevant information) do take effect, and the fuse controller state machine behaves identically between FPF and non-FPF regions. The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (âSBFEâ), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what âsecured burnâ truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just donât know what the âsecuredâ adjective really means here. Note PLM , HS , ucode , â¦; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon . Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Letâs talk some more about voltage glitching. Voltage fault injection Much has been said about VFI, and Iâll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the cardâs own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus. The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap. With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence: Remove card power Apply card power Start a timer (âglitch timerâ) as soon as NVVDD crosses a threshold Execute a proposed voltage waveform by issuing a PWMVID signal, aligned to the glitch timer Observe card behavior, repeat from step 1 as needed My setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later. For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability). Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, Iâve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive. More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if youâre interested. For now, letâs take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages: Sense RIR, as required by the fuse macro Sense (from fuse macro into readout register) control rows Latch control rows into control row-derived option words Sense remaining rows Latch regular fuse values into their option words Parse FF chain Latch FF chain values into their option words These hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when CMD_READ works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Letâs take a look at 3 interesting glitch states. 1. All fuses sensed as zero Commanded PWMVID duty Â· 59.58% / 0.8333% Expected NVVDD Â· simulated Issued duty and modeled NVVDD The orange series is commanded PWMVID duty after the MCU ADC's NVVDD 225 mV boot trigger at t=0, then a marked gap to 200â1015 ms. Pulse intervals: 210.000â1010.000 ms. The teal series is simulated NVVDD, with a modeled boot rise through 225 mV and slew-limited responses to the commanded pulses. It is not a same-run voltage capture. This attempt had 668/672 zero option reads; the section's 669/672 example is a different capture. 200 400 600 800 1000 t=0 NVVDD â¥225 mV MCU ADC trigger Pulse 1: 210.000â1010.000 ms, 800 ms duration 900 mV 297.8 mV ms after t=0; left gap omits 0â200 ms Some glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controllerâs CRC status was 0x00 (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as 2080 (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPUâs PRI ring was held in reset. This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional. 2. RIR read disrupted Commanded PWMVID duty Â· 59.58% / 0.8333% Expected NVVDD Â· simulated Issued duty and modeled NVVDD The orange series is commanded PWMVID duty after the MCU ADC's NVVDD 225 mV boot trigger at t=0, then a marked gap to 977â1008 ms. Pulse intervals: 980.000â1005.000 ms. The teal series is simulated NVVDD, with a modeled boot rise through 225 mV and slew-limited responses to the commanded pulses. It is not a same-run voltage capture. The row-18-only readback recurred on a second boot; RIR involvement is a hypothesis. 978 980 985 990 995 1000 1005 t=0 NVVDD â¥225 mV MCU ADC trigger Pulse 1: 980.000â1005.000 ms, 25 ms duration 900 mV 297.8 mV ms after t=0; left gap omits 0â977 ms Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself. 3. Goldilockâs glitch Commanded PWMVID duty Â· 59.58% / 0.8333% Expected NVVDD Â· simulated Issued duty and modeled NVVDD The orange series is commanded PWMVID duty after the MCU ADC's NVVDD 225 mV boot trigger at t=0, then a marked gap to 978â992 ms. Pulse intervals: 979.940â981.940 ms, 983.940â985.940 ms, 987.940â989.940 ms. The teal series is simulated NVVDD, with a modeled boot rise through 225 mV and slew-limited responses to the commanded pulses. It is not a same-run voltage capture. 978 980 982 984 986 988 990 992 t=0 NVVDD â¥225 mV MCU ADC trigger Pulse 1: 979.940â981.940 ms, 2 ms duration Pulse 2: 983.940â985.940 ms, 2 ms duration Pulse 3: 987.940â989.940 ms, 2 ms duration 900 mV 297.8 mV ms after t=0; left gap omits 0â978 ms The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this: Signal Initial readback PCI ID and access 20c2 ; BAR0 and the PRI ring respond FUSECTRL 0xe0040000 ( IDLE ) CRC_ STATUS 0x55 (both halves parsed without errors) DISABLE_ SW_ OVERRIDE 0 OPT_ SECURED_ BURN_ FEATURE_ ENABLE 0 ENABLE_ FUSE_ PROGRAM 0 FUSECTRL/FUSEOPT privilege masks 0xffffffff for both Raw rows 0 and 1 Both still 0x53557c3d , unchanged from before the glitch At this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would ever be zero, given itâs 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so). Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a âcanaryâ fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses. However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us âshadowâ most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems weâre stuck. At least thatâs what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I havenât tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, except DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0! With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing. At this point, all thatâs left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored. End results Framebuffer unlock On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage. Compute unlock The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100! FP16 FMA throughput TFLOP/s software-unlocked CMP 170HX 50.129 TFLOP/s 0.69Ã retail A100 retail A100 72.488 TFLOP/s 1.00Ã hardware-unlocked CMP 170HX 85.861 TFLOP/s 1.18Ã retail A100 0 30 60 90 ProjectPhysX OpenCL-Benchmark FP16 half2 FMA: software-unlocked CMP 170HX, 50.129 TFLOP/s; retail A100, 72.488 TFLOP/s; hardware-unlocked CMP 170HX, 85.861 TFLOP/s. Retail A100 is the 1.00 times reference. PCIe generation The only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant. NVLink Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if youâre bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair. On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. Iâm sure your clanker can figure it out ;) While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIAâs NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned! Future directions With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But whatâs more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals. References Jon Pry, A Canary in the Crypto Mine: Defeating Stack Protection in a GPU Secure Coprocessor (2026). Amogh Munikote, cmpunlocker (2026). Otto Bittner et al., The Forgotten Threat of Voltage Glitching: A Case Study on Nvidia Tegra X2 SoCs (2021). NVIDIA, US9230678B2: Integrated circuit having an enhanced fuseless fuse structure (2016). TSMC, TEF07F32X32HD18_PHRM_C180518 electrical fuse datasheet, rev. 120A (2018). hexkyz and SciresM, Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon (2021). TechPowerUp, NVIDIA GA100 GPU specifications . GA100VFI source repository . Footnotes Anecdotally, out of the 10 specimens of CMP 170HX 8 GB I have examined, only one has shipped with only 64 GB usable, the rest all have a functional framebuffer size of 80 GB. â© Although the Canary in the Crypto Mine paper claims a stable 80 GB on the 10 GB SKU, very few, if any, cards in the wild have been able to achieve this, and solid evidence is scarce. It remains plausible that some number of 10 GB SKUs really do come shipped with 80 GB on-board, however the percentage seems very low according to the community. Most âunstableâ 80 GB unlocks are explained with a combination of L2 caching and memory aliasing over a true 40 GB framebuffer. â© Enabling NVLink further requires a very small hardware mod due to a missing component on the 170HX PCB, Iâll talk more about this later. â© Untested. â© â© 2 â© 3 â All writing Back to top â RSS

title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America

And It's Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America - The Autopian Skip to content Youtube Facebook-f Twitter Instagram Rss Sign in Register Sign out Account Sign in Register Sign out Account Night Panel Disable Night Panel News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Menu News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Home » Scion Is Back! And It’s Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America Scion Is Back! And It’s Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America By Leslie Hanna November 10, 2026 11:07 am 107 Comments When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back. Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features. “Okei,” let’s go. Toyota Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future. With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses. Toyota The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard. Toyota It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. Initially, the KEI 01 is only going to be available in a low-volume, niche pilot program entirely focused on fleet usage beginning in late 2027. Depending on performance and owner feedback, availability of the KEI-01 may eventually be expanded, but no further information is available from Toyota at the time.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by The Autopian (@theautopian) The Hybrid Side-By-Side Toyota Two other mobility concepts accompany the KEI-01 in the Scion by Toyota lineup, the SxS Concept and the BXE Concept. The SxS Concept was unveiled at the 2025 SEMA Show as a purpose-built side-by-side all-terrain vehicle ( click here for our coverage). Developed by Toyota North America, the off-road concept is outfitted with a turbocharged four-cylinder from the Tacoma making in the realm of 300hp. You won’t have to worry about your turbo spool scaring away local fauna, as it is equipped with a “Silent Mode,” which allows the driver to switch from the boisterous internal combustion system to a much more civilised fully electric driving mode. Unlike the KEI-01, the SxS Concept is still just that – a concept, with no current plans to have a version available to the public. Toyota Last, but not least, is the BKE Concept. The BKE concept is entirely focused on personal mobility in the outdoors, filling the gap between the utility of the KEI-01 and the pure performance of the SxS Concept. Its small form factor and rugged tires make it an ideal off-roader for traversing narrow paths while being portable enough to stow away when not in use or easily tote around in the back of a car. title: What constant surveillance is doing to children and parents
AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
body_text: AMD’s Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast - by George Cozma Chips and Cheese Subscribe Sign in AMD’s Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast George Cozma Nov 10, 2026 54 2 7 Share Hello you fine Internet folks, Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture. Hope y’all enjoy! Overview From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core. Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2. At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4. Branch Prediction Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor. The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5. Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache. When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB. When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity. The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor. Instruction Fetch Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters. Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things. Execution Engine The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of. On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs. AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost. On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well. Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2. The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed. Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue. The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330. The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency. Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB. L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns. Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle. Load/Store Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify. EPYC 9686F (Zen 6) STLF test EPYC 9996 (Zen 6c) STLF test Zen 5 STLF test A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5. SPEC CPU 2026 Performance The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3. The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point. The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian. Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage. Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point. Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share. The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips. The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher. Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow. The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory. The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy. The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow. The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory. Final Words The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5. However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior. The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs. AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs. 54 2 7 Share Previous Next Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Nathan Gabriel 1d thanks for this! title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave
body_text: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave (Native Approach) | Serge Gatezh Skip to main content $ Serge Gatezh Posts Projects Talks About Contact > Posts > Projects > Talks > About > Contact ~/posts/macos-secure-enclave-ssh-keys cat macos-secure-enclave-ssh-keys.md Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave (Native Approach) February 12, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 by Serge Gatezh 8 min read 1534 words How to keep SSH keys in the macOS Secure Enclave, with Touch ID on every use and no third-party apps. Update, November 11, 2026: I’ve since switched to Secretive , which keeps keys in the Secure Enclave with a much better prompt. Part 2 is coming. I’ve also corrected one error, marked below. I’ve been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in ~/.ssh/ , protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers. Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine. This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn’t be enough for you or anybody else really). So I finally decided to do something about it. TL;DR I have decided to NOT go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can’t live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise. The Options After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys: Native macOS Secure Enclave â no third-party apps, built into the OS Secretive â third-party app that stores keys in Secure Enclave YubiKey â hardware security key with FIDO2 support 1Password / Bitwarden â store keys in an encrypted vault, use their SSH agent I already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it’s still a software solution â the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used. What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised. That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first â no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain. What is Secure Enclave SSH? Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac’s chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves. When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk. The workflow is surprisingly similar to regular SSH keys: Aspect Regular SSH Key Secure Enclave Key Where private key lives ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (a file) Secure Enclave What’s on disk Actual private key Just a reference (useless without this Mac) Setup on remote server Copy public key to authorized_keys Same Connecting Just works Touch ID prompt, then works Setting It Up Step 1: Create the Secure Enclave Key macOS provides the sc_auth command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too. sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio Breaking this down: -l "ssh-MacBook" â a label for your reference (only visible locally) -k p-256-ne â NIST P-256 curve, n on- e xportable (the key can never leave Secure Enclave) -t bio â require bio metric (Touch ID) for every use You’ll be prompted for Touch ID to create the key. Problem 1: Touch ID Error When I first ran this command, I got a scary error: Error: Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-25293 "Failed to generate keypair" (errKCAuthFailed / errSecAuthFailed: / Authorization/Authentication failed.) UserInfo={..., NSUnderlyingError=... "Failed to get bio catacomb UUID for user 502." ...} Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings â Touch ID & Password , the command worked fine. You can verify the key was created: sc_auth list-ctk-identities Output: Key Type Public Key Hash Prot Label Common Name Valid To Valid p-256-ne A71277F0BC5825A7B3576D014F31282A866EF3BC bio ssh-MacBook ssh-MacBook 2027-01-26, 10:18 YES Step 2: Export the Key Handle Now we need to create a “key handle” file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key â it’s just a reference that tells SSH “go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this.” ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N "" When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it’s not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates id_ecdsa_sk_rk and id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub in your current directory. Move them to your SSH directory: mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/ Step 3: Configure SSH to Use the Secure Enclave Provider Add this to your ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc ): export SSH_SK_PROVIDER = /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib Reload your shell: source ~/.zshrc Problem 2: Outdated Commands Everywhere If you search for “macOS Secure Enclave SSH” online, you’ll find a lot of guides telling you to run ssh-add -K . Don’t. It’s deprecated: WARNING: The -K and -A flags are deprecated and have been replaced by the --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain flags, respectively. And even the new flags don’t work for Secure Enclave keys â they’re for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The SSH_SK_PROVIDER environment variable is the correct approach. Step 4: Get Your Public Key cat ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub Output: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh: That ssh: at the end is the comment. The key’s FIDO2 application ID is stored inside the key itself (the last field of the base64 part). ssh-keygen -K copies it into the comment, so the line shows it twice. You can replace the comment with anything when copying to authorized_keys ; the key stays the same: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... macbook-secure-enclave Correction, November 11, 2026: An earlier version said the trailing ssh: was the FIDO2 application ID. It’s the comment; the application ID is stored inside the key. Thanks to computerfriend on Hacker News for pointing it out. Step 5: Copy to Your Server ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub user@your-server Or manually paste the public key (with your comment) into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Step 6: Configure ~/.ssh/config Problem 3: SSH Doesn’t Find the Key After setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password. The verbose output ( ssh -vvv ) showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key: debug1: Offering public key: /Users/sergii/.ssh/id_rsa RSA SHA256:... The problem: SSH doesn’t automatically look for files named id_ecdsa_sk_rk . It only auto-discovers standard names like id_rsa , id_ed25519 , id_ecdsa . The fix is to explicitly add it to your ~/.ssh/config : Host * IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default. â ï¸ Note: If you’re using 1Password’s SSH agent ( IdentityAgent ), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing. Step 7: Test It ssh user@your-server You should get a Touch ID prompt, then connect. The Ugly Touch ID Prompt Touch ID prompt One thing I’m not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says “ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue” instead of something friendly like “SSH wants to use your key.” This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit â a low-level framework that Apple hasn’t polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, Secretive provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood. Why Touch ID for Everything? I initially thought about creating two keys â one with Touch ID for “important” servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations). But then I realized: without -t bio , malware could use my key silently. With -t bio , I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility. So my recommendation if you’re planning to store your SSH keys this way: just use -t bio for everything. If it ever gets annoying, you can always create a second key later. The Catch: No Backups Secure Enclave keys are tied to your specific Mac. If your Mac dies, the keys die with it. That’s by design: the key can’t be exported, so it can’t be backed up either. Keep more than one key instead. Add your Secure Enclave key AND a backup key (from a YubiKey, or another Mac) to your servers’ authorized_keys . If one device is lost, you still have access via the other. Final Thoughts It seems to be a proper way to store your SSH keys securely, and it is way better than storing them on your hard drive. With the implementation above you get: â Private key literally cannot be stolen (it’s in hardware) â Every SSH operation requires Touch ID (I know when my key is used) â No third-party apps needed â Works with existing authorized_keys workflow However, I’ve been somewhat surprised by the ugliness of the UI. Not sure why Apple released such an unpolished thing. In each and every presentation they have a section on security (where their Apple logo becomes an Apple lock), so I was expecting an actual aesthetically appealing look for their security features. It is definitely not the case. My sense of beauty is not compatible with this ugliness, so I will be looking into other solutions to store my SSH keys in Secure Enclave such as Secretive . I also still need a backup option in case anything happens to my Mac. ls --related Docker Desktop Disk Full on macOS: The 1 TB Default and the Dev Containers Cache Sep 2026 MCP: What It Is and Why It Matters (by Addy Osmani) Jul 2025 ← Publishing Multi-Platform Docker Images to GitHub Container Registry Docker Desktop Disk Full on macOS: The 1 TB Default and the Dev Containers Cache → ./comments --list Please enable JavaScript to view the comments. title: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?
body_text: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming? nathan.rs Writing X Github LinkedIn ☾ Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming? Nathan Barry November 9, 2026 Introduction Thinking loops How Astra fixed the loops Choosing v is a linear program Results A steering vector does the same job Limitations and what’s next Citation Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this weight-space programming . In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%. 1 Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself. This article appeared on Hacker News. Link to the discussion here . Thinking loops # Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in thinking loops , repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer. The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%. Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 GSM8K IFEval Hit token limit Base 7.9 13.8 21.0 93.0% Astra’s edit 48.1 67.1 62.3 33.1% On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked. How Astra fixed the loops # Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the residual stream (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way. Finding the loop direction # Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the loop direction $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops. Editing the weights # Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called down_proj ). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$: $$x \leftarrow x + Wh, \qquad Wh = \sum_j h_j \, w_j$$ So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token. Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it: $$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$ At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model away from looping whenever it’s used. Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a rank-1 change: $$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$ At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes. That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems: Edit on layers 15 and 19 Accuracy Base model ~9% Every column, α = 1 33% Every column, α = 2 43% Every column, α = 3 48% Random direction (control) 12.5% Top 64 columns, α = 6 55% Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text. Where the time went # The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing. The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything. 2 Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours. Choosing v is a linear program # Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities. I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: looping tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and productive tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts, 3 and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$: $$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$ In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable. Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts. To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero. 4 That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute. 5 Results # I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a heuristic direction : label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning. Changed weights GSM8K test MATH-500 IFEval Base model 0 14.1 7.0 22.9 Astra’s edit 130,188 68.2 50.9 61.9 LP, Astra’s direction 16,291 69.6 51.7 59.7 LP, heuristic direction 16,271 65.4 47.8 60.4 With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there. A few other things showed up: The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7. Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$ A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model. A steering vector does the same job # An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way. 6 So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token. The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a steering vector , a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token. The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths: Steering strength (× the LP edit’s average push) Dev set MATH-500 0.5× 51.6 1× 57.8 50.8 2× 31.2 For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem. At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart. The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time. Limitations and what’s next # This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it. Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece. Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream. 7 If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing. Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub . Citation # Please cite this work as: Barry, Nathan. "Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?" nathan.rs (Nov 2026). https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp. Or use the BibTex citation: @article{barry2026wslp, title = "Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?", author = "Barry, Nathan", journal = "nathan.rs", year = "2026", month = "Nov", url = "https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp" } Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, Sparks of Weight-Space Programming , MIT CSAIL, 2026. The logs are released under CC BY 4.0, and everything about Astra’s run in this post comes from them.  ↩︎ Astra’s full run took 158 turns and 20.3 hours, 4.7 of them an outage. 19 forward passes failed and weren’t counted against its budget. The full breakdown is in the write-up .  ↩︎ A token counts as repeated if the 16 tokens ending at it already appeared earlier in the answer. A loop starts at the first point after which at least 80% of the remaining tokens are repeats. Looping tokens are repeats at least 64 tokens into a loop. Productive tokens come at least 256 tokens before it, or anywhere in an answer that finished.  ↩︎ Each column is ranked by $|v_j|$ times the standard deviation of $h_j$, roughly how much it adds along $u$ at a typical token.  ↩︎ PDHG (primal-dual hybrid gradient) only needs matrix-vector products, so all the token constraints fit on the GPU at once, and it returns an exactly sparse $v$.  ↩︎ A linear probe on layer 15’s activations can tell looping tokens from productive ones once a loop is under way (AUC 0.93), but much less well at the point where it starts (0.73).  ↩︎ Or whether you can make it sound like her .  ↩︎ Last modified: November 12, 2026 nathan.rs - © 2025 Nathan Barry

title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
body_text: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude Introduction Performance and efficiency Coding Cybersecurity Science and engineering Safety and alignment Data privacy Availability November 9, 2026 Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 [1] Introduction [2] Performance and efficiency [3] Science and engineering [4] Safety and alignment [5] Availability We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card . When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models). Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 Benchmark performance. Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task.
