At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 scores 66.4%, ahead of Opus 5.5 at Max effort (64.4%) for less than one-tenth of the cost per task. Coding Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests. As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below). Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks: Vercel Shopify Datadog Unity Uber Oracle iGent Snowflake Cognition Vercel Shopify Datadog Unity Uber Oracle iGent Snowflake Cognition Quote “The model is in my head. It understands the intent behind every prompt I’ve given it. I haven’t had to say ‘No, I meant…’ a single time. Projects we’ve been pushing along with other models for weeks got finished and approved by our teammates in a few days with Claude Fable 5.2, and the humans reviewing its code had less to say.” Company Vercel Author Joe Haddad, Member of Technical Staff Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is great for taking a loose idea and refining it. Its answers are really well-considered, and within a few turns I can almost always say ‘ok, go do that,’ and trust that it’ll complete it with little intervention. It feels like working with another staff-level engineer.” Company Shopify Author Tom Pritchard, Staff Engineer Quote “You can just throw Claude Fable 5.2 at new, ambiguous systems it has never seen before, and it will figure out how to actually work within them. It’s almost like an incident commander that can send out faster models to get quick signals and coordinate, which removes that burden from me as an operator.” Company Datadog Author Matt Lee, Senior Staff Engineer Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 can complete tasks that previous models struggled with. The clearest examples so far are building higher-quality 3D scenes from scratch and rebuilding an experience from a visual reference. It’s very strong on the harder game-dev tasks, where it keeps iterating and improving instead of getting stuck.” Company Unity Author Sam Zhang, Creative Technologist Quote “I had Claude Fable 5.2 run a 10–12 hour security audit. It sent out about 170 reviewer agents and came back with a write-up, fix pull requests and a policy proposal. It works until the job is actually complete instead of stopping at a plausible checkpoint. Its self-correction and honesty about gaps impressed me. At High effort, I’d use this over what I run today for long unattended audits and doc-heavy work.” Company Uber Author Andrew Mager, Staff Engineer, Agentic Systems Quote “In one test combining country debt summaries, repayment history, and regional benchmarks, Claude Fable 5.2 generated SQL that returned the expected results. The SQL generated by two other models also ran successfully, but incorrectly summed country-level summary amounts, producing values 5–8x the expected amounts. Getting these business calculations right is why we see value in using Fable 5.2 for enterprise SQL generation.” Company Oracle Author Liyu Gong, Senior Manager of Machine Learning Quote “In a single session, Claude Fable 5.2 built a hypervisor, the software that walls off virtual computers sharing one machine. Its core is mathematically proven to keep them apart. More than 3,500 machine-checked proofs cover every case, not just the ones you test. It’s the first model I’ve seen break a problem this large into pieces it can prove, fit them together, and keep taking on more ambitious work. A very clear upgrade from Fable 5.1.” Company iGent Author Sean Ward, Co-Founder and CEO Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is the strongest model we have measured on data-eng-bench, our open-source benchmark of 103 data-engineering tasks. It solved tasks consistently across repeated runs and passed every interactive coding task we gave it.” Company Snowflake Author Bala Kasiviswanathan, VP of AI and Developer Experience Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 says it doesn’t know things instead of hallucinating. At one point it told me its last estimate was wrong and that it wouldn’t give a number until it had measured the change. Very impressive!” Company Cognition Author Adhyyan Sekhsaria, Member of Technical Staff Cybersecurity Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.² CVE Rediscovery Accuracy vs. cost Mythos 5.2 Opus 5.5 Mythos 5.1 55 60 65 70 75 80 85 90 95 0 Advisories found (%) 0.10 0.20 0.50 1 2 5 10 Cost per attempt (USD, log scale) Low Med High Xhigh Max CVE Rediscovery is an internal cybersecurity evaluation that assesses how many published CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) a model can independently find when given a snapshot of the project before a CVE was fixed. Our October 2026 run against 1,829 CVEs showed Claude Mythos 5.2 outperformed Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 at every effort level. Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program , which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security , which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP. Rubrik Mozilla Rubrik Mozilla Quote “We have worked closely with Anthropic’s new model, Claude Mythos 5.2, to do a next round of high-fidelity threat discovery and elimination within our own systems for potential issues we did not uncover with earlier Mythos models. The output is more readable and empowered our team to spot-check faster and more easily. We built our Code Guardian harness with Mythos 5.1, and we’d switch to Mythos 5.2 to give our customers more powerful cyber capabilities.” Company Rubrik Author Arvind Nithrakashyap, Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer Quote “Claude Mythos 5.2 is astonishingly good. We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns.” Company Mozilla Author Brian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer Science and engineering Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas. Theoretical physics Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics. Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here . Protein folding Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid , can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together. Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies: Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Quote “This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.” Company Dyno Therapeutics Author Sam Sinai, Cofounder and Head of AI Quote “Large protein assemblies, including capsids, remain an open problem for protein modeling, due to the complexity of accurately predicting and positioning the structures of dozens of individual macromolecules, not to mention the inordinately high computational costs involved. Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.” Company Columbia University Author Mohammed AlQuraishi, Assistant Professor of Systems Biology and Computer Science Quote “Biohub’s goal in open-sourcing ESMFold2 was to enable the scientific community to build on the biology it has learned. We are excited to see Claude prototype a new sampling procedure that enables predictions of large, symmetric complexes such as AAV capsids—a protein used to deliver gene therapies. We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.” Company Biohub Author Zeming Lin, Principal Research Scientist Mathematics Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas. Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem , performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, and built its own ways to coordinate.⁴ It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30. Read more about the formalization here . Fermat’s Last Theorem proof formalization Completion over time Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 0 0.2 0.4 0.6 0.8 1 Completion (0–1, weighted share of statements proved) 0 6 12 18 24 30 Time elapsed (hours) Resumed with 12 more hours 0.86 1.00 0.26 0.27 Formalizing the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in the mathematical programming language Lean. Each line shows the proportion of the full formalization that Fable 5.2 (green line) and Opus 5.5 (orange line) had completed over 30 hours with about 1,000 agents, and a single run per model. At the dashed line (18 hours), both teams resumed from their last save with 12 more hours. Hardware and robotics Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world , showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots. Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode , a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards. Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here . Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots. RoboDojo (average) Max score by model Gemini 4 Argon GPT-6 Astra Fable 5.1 Opus 5.5 Fable 5.2 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 Average success rate (%) Gemini 4 Argon (our run; High effort) GPT-6 Astra (our run; Max effort) Fable 5.1 (Max effort) Opus 5.5 (Max effort) Fable 5.2 (Max effort) 34.2 29.8 27.6 39.4 64.9 RoboDojo Sim tests control of a simulated two-arm robot. Scores are based on our internal runs for each model using the highest available effort level. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%) and Fable 5.1 (27.6%). Research and analysis Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses. Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2: Jump Trading Balyasny Asset Management Discovered Materials IMC Harvey Fundamental Research Labs XTX Markets Box Jump Trading Balyasny Asset Management Discovered Materials IMC Harvey Fundamental Research Labs XTX Markets Box Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is incredible at playing every major role within a research system: defining questions, interpreting, coordinating, and of course finding and implementing the key ideas. Definitely one of the strongest on taste and judgment that we’ve seen. In an internal research automation benchmark, it achieved a full 10% lower error than the next best model.” Company Jump Trading Author Lucas Baker, Head of LLM R&D Quote “In a recent evaluation, we asked Claude Fable 5.2 to investigate how one organization tested a new integration in its core technology systems. It traced the answer to the right sources and didn’t overstate what the evidence showed. It also flagged that the question’s framing could be misleading. In investment research, that restraint makes clear what remains unknown and where the market may be mispricing risk or opportunity.” Company Balyasny Asset Management Author Ashish Malik, AI Researcher Quote “Phonon calculations are one of the most expensive routine steps in computational materials science, which is why labs often skip stability checks when screening new materials. Claude Fable 5.2 made Quantum ESPRESSO’s phonon code about 36 times faster on average than stock on the same GPU, taking our 13 benchmark cases from 3.3 hours to under four minutes. That beats Fable 5.1’s speedup by 3–4 times.” Company Discovered Materials Author Akash Ramdas, Co-Founder Quote “With Fable 5.1 we saw the first glimmers of a model coming up with truly innovative research ideas. Claude Fable 5.2 continues that trend. It had the same insight we were impressed with from Fable 5.1 and then came up with a second, entirely new angle. It achieved new best scores on three of the four quant research problems we’ve finished. We’d like to use it for high-impact, long-running research tasks, or for coordinating teams of other models.” Company IMC Author Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer Quote “In an I-9 compliance review, Claude Fable 5.2 gave the client clearer direction than Fable 5.1. It identified the employees needing immediate attention and explained how to correct each issue and who should act. It’s an exciting improvement in the model’s ability to give practical legal guidance.” Company Harvey Author Niko Grupen, Head of AI Research Quote “On one task, Claude Fable 5.2 had to pull a company’s financials out of its 10-K into a forecasting model, and the template didn’t say whether a metric should be the reported figure or calculated. It inferred the author’s intent from the cell formatting, caught that the regional numbers didn’t sum to the reported total, and got every cell right. Better judgment calls like that are the main reason it scored 91% on our eval versus 86% for the next best model.” Company Fundamental Research Labs Author Jeffrey Liu, Member of Technical Staff Quote “In our quantitative research work, Claude Fable 5.2 delivered very strong improvements versus Fable 5.1, especially in the setup with multiple coordinating agents. Its maths research capabilities represent another meaningful advance, too.” Company XTX Markets Author Alex Gerko, Founder and CEO Quote “Before putting AI to work across workflows, you need to trust its approach and conclusions. In our testing, Claude Fable 5.2 identified inconsistencies, drew on context across entire document sets, and adjusted recommendations based on relevant evidence. For example, when reviewing files attached to a loan application, it flagged that the salary deposits and the bank statement’s balance didn’t match, so the underwriter could focus on what to check.” Company Box Author Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products Safety and alignment No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute , Frontier Design , and METR . See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁵ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing. Alignment testing We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models). We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁶ Automated behavioral audit Overall misaligned behavior score Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4 Score (1–10, lower is better) Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 3.28 2.79 3.10 2.67 Overall score from our automated behavioral audit, a composite of many undesirable behaviors including cooperation with human misuse and autonomous actions across a range of scenarios. Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card for full details. We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences). We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1. The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss. Safeguards Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas. AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators. Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report , which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features). Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe. Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form . Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring. Availability Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform. This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here . Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program . Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security , powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program . Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs. Edit 11 November: Amended a sentence and added a footnote to the “Mathematical formalization” subsection to more accurately describe the information we provided to the model. Footnotes 1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures , a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities. 2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card ). 3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus , EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension , SymProFold , CapBuild , MoLPC , CombFold , Uni-Fold Symmetry , Apodex Discovery , and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 ( PDB:1LP3 ). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2. 4 As described in our accompanying post , we “gave the agents a list of 60 statements, a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, the definitions those statements use, and 47 proved lemmas from our earlier formalization, and assigned lead and helper roles. We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.” 5 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication. 6 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards. title: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
body_text: After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings | Blog | VulnCheck Products Government Resources Community Company Partners Sign In / Join Sign In Go back November 9, 2026 After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings Patrick Garrity in/patrickmgarrity/ ai cve kev VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB Join Now Key Takeaways: Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild. Of Anthropicâs 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed. Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation. Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn. Anthropicâs claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings. Anthropicâs OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question. We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality. As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign. That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities. If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts: Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15 Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28 The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8 So let's look at the resultsâ¦ Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches. My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked. After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs. For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself. The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980) Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look. Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as âTrue Positivesâ. The trend since my September update is even more telling: September 8 November 2 Change Total findings 26,153 37,966 +11,813 Made public 2,736 (10.5%) 7,349 (19.4%) +4,613 Fixed 202 217 +15 Withdrawn 245 419 +174 Duplicates 2 1,670 +1,668 Claimed true positive rate 91.4% 94.2% +2.8 pts In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning. You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter. Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk. So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid." In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem. curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg , who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them. Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden. This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability. It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing. curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead. Takeaways After Seven Months AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile. About VulnCheck VulnCheck is helping organizations not just to solve the vulnerability prioritization challenge - weâre working to help equip any product manager, CSIRT/PSIRT or SecOps team and Threat Hunting team to get faster and more accurate with infinite efficiency using VulnCheck solutions. We knew that we needed better data, faster across the board, in our industry. So thatâs what we deliver to the market. Weâre going to continue to deliver key insights on vulnerability management, exploitation and major trends we can extrapolate from our dataset to continuously support practitioners. Are you interested in learning more? If so, VulnCheck's Exploit & Vulnerability Intelligence has broad threat actor coverage. Register and demo our data today. Ready to get Started? 10, 2026 Research Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri Read the technical paper Share Copied How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signalâs cryptographic protocol â long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, weâre sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verificationâmathematically proving code runs correctly without flawsâis the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. How we verified Signal AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signalâs security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human â just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties â such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised â down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex. Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks â a task that historically takes expert teams years â proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified. To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. In AlphaProof Code, AI agents help users write a specification, then autonomously prove that the implementation meets it. Every proof is checked by Lean to verify the agents' work. While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion. Using AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees. Ehren Kret Chief Technology Officer of Signal While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees. The future of security Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats. Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software. Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender , formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work. We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below. Integrations Contribute Blog TS TypeScript Python Search Theme GitHub Discord Search Ctrl K Cancel All posts November 9, 2026 5 min read Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider Two Amazon engineers swapped Claude Sonnet 4.6 for a decision model in one of the world's biggest internal ticketing systems. Carr Onstott , Mehul Jaiswal , Strands Agents Team For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank. Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider , a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well at 98% less cost . This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year. Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below. Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels. A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog. We started with the original Strands Decider 2B . On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets. We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB, and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from S3 before start-up. Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod. Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message: BEDROCK : Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called. DUAL : Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results. DECIDER : Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called. What we measured Claude Sonnet 4.6 Strands Decider E4B % Improvement Average time per call 4,215 ms 897 ms 78% Input tokens per ticket 6,554 2,009 Output tokens per ticket 170 1 Total tokens, per ticket 6,724 2,010 70% The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit. Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%. What it costs At published us-east-1 on-demand prices: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint) Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, ml.g5.xlarge ) Price $3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokens $1.408 per instance-hour Per ticket $0.0222 about $0.0005 Per million tickets about $22,200 about $500 Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction. These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now. One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs. Our lessons This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job. The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change. The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes . title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
body_text: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN.net] LWN .net News from the source Content Weekly Edition Archives Search Kernel Security Events calendar Unread comments LWN FAQ Write for us Edition Return to the Front page User: Password: | | Log in / Subscribe / Register Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN subscriber-only content] Welcome to LWN.net The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN . Thank you for visiting LWN.net! By Joe Brockmeier November 10, 2026 Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms. Synaptics and Displaylink The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu. The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities. A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices. Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software. Vino He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. " If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome. " He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings , but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve. Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue. He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian . He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics: The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK. From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions. Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the " intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink ", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than " have the situation become more formal later ". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK. Cease and desist On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice . The letter stated that Lothian had not " substantially responded " to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with " public statements and further development activities ". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that " cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation ", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work. Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of " any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent ", withdrawing submissions of materials " made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization ", and to identify in writing every location " in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed ". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands. Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had " never lit a panel ", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko. On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. " A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns. " He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to " reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software ". He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims " interact with our respective OIN commitments ", and expressed a desire to sort things out with Synaptics constructively. " I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities ". Lothian did not think he could " reasonably provide the signed undertaking " Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work. Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned: As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now we are escalating as we deem appropriate. The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be " single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology ". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization. Bateman sent a follow-up letter , dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking " monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts ". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with. Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts " ideally with someone qualified to help me read them ". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that " DisplayLink is not a member of OIN " and none of its technology was licensable through OIN. OIN to the rescue? Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory . In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion. OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition , but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs (" a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal ") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components. I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation. Status Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of the components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. " Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics. " Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: " You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?' " For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users. to post comments Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 10, 2026 16:15 UTC (Tue) by paulj (subscriber, #341) [ Link ] (6 responses) GB2485613B seems ludicrous. Its claim appear to be no more than using image compression (in general!) to display to a screen over a general purpose data transport, such as USB, Ethernet, etc., wherein the compressed data is received, demuxed from whatever containing headers, stored, decompressed and displayed. Come on Synaptics... Nonsense. And GB2484736B seems to be about using a Haar wavelet/transform to compress and decompress an image, by way of encoding/decoding sub-groups of the image. I don't know enough about image compression and Haar's transform to know if there is anything novel about, but knowledge of using Haar's transform for image compression goes back to at least the 1970s - e.g., see US4224678A from 1976. The idea of applying compression to an image in sub-groups of the image is surely also long described (??). Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 11, 2026 11:53 UTC (Wed) by LtWorf (subscriber, #124958) [ Link ] (5 responses) The entire point of patents is to threaten people. They are aware that the patents should have never been granted, but also know how expensive that is. Anyway europe never had software patents so I am not sure what the status is in UK currently. Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 11, 2026 11:56 UTC (Wed) by paulj (subscriber, #341) [ Link ] (4 responses) Europe doesn't have software patents, but it has patents for algorithms and software once running on computer devices. So it has software patents. Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 11, 2026 12:19 UTC (Wed) by smoogen (subscriber, #97) [ Link ] (2 responses) This is one of those things that should be written in more depth by someone. People pull out the "Europe doesn't have software patents" over and over again.. but then you see that you can patent certain items which are definitely the same as software patents... Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 11, 2026 21:27 UTC (Wed) by willy (subscriber, #9762) [ Link ] (1 responses) I think this is covered by the maxim of "never take legal advice from an engineer". ie 90% of the comments in this thread. Yes, you're very smart. No, you don't understand that this word means something different in legal than in English. Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 12, 2026 12:37 UTC (Thu) by paulj (subscriber, #341) [ Link ] I don't remember the details anymore, but there was a lot of discussion circa 20, 25 years ago, when there was some kind of Directive proposed - wikipedia suggests it was to have essentially enacted existing EPO practice - which effectively allows software patents, once combined with a computer. Many of us wrote letters to our MEPs about this. Seems we succeeded in blocking that directive. However, we never succeeded in changing the existing practice - where the clause in the European Patent Convention that bans software patents has this little ", as such" at the end which the EPO and basically all other national patent offices use to effectively allow software patents as long as the claimant adds "... on a computer" to their patent. So we are still stuck with that. Ciarán O'Riordan, who has been known to comment here, would know a lot more, with a lot better clarity. Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Reverse engineering Posted Nov 11, 2026 2:50 UTC (Wed) by felixfix (subscriber, #242) [ Link ] Long long ago (1980?), our computer supplier Datapoint came out with a new networked operating system, but would not tell us what the assembler system calls were; they expected everyone to use their high level scripting language. There were 6 of us programmers in a company of roughly 100 employees, and supposedly we were Datapoint's second biggest customer. My boss was more than a little miffed. He told me to do nothing for the next month or two but document their system calls. I ended up writing a terrible networked space shootemup which worked fine for reverse engineering, and ported enough of our system to the new OS to make the new OS seem worthwhile. He showed up at their HQ with my documentation and said they could either provide us with official documentation under NDA or we would publish what I had found. They caved in and we got their official documentation. As far as I remember, I had everything correct that we cared about, although one glitch I had found turned out to be a bug which they fixed about six months later. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 18:03 UTC (Tue) by mebrown (subscriber, #7960) [ Link ] (5 responses) The ENTIRE point of patents is to publish in the open the methods used in sufficient detail as to teach others how to use the invention. Their claim that this code does this is just ludicrous when their actual patent does that already. (quite aside from the separate discussion on if they have a valid patent at all). They have a patent on hardware. Even if all this code is published, they still have that hardware patent and can prevent anybody else from producing such hardware. Acting this way to prevent a real driver from being developed is incredibly short sighted of them as it does nothing to affect the actual underlying hardware. As somebody who holds over 50 patents myself and sits on my company patent committee, this is a total face-palm for me. Just misunderstanding and stupidity all around. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 20:30 UTC (Tue) by IanKelling (subscriber, #89418) [ Link ] (4 responses) > Their claim that this code does this is just ludicrous when their actual patent does that already. I don't really see where you are coming from. The patent gives knowledge but restricts the use of that knowledge in various ways. This is the general premise of patents that you seem to be calling it ludicrous, and I don't follow. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:21 UTC (Tue) by roc (subscriber, #30627) [ Link ] (2 responses) Maybe it's clearer to point out that the following sentence is incompatible with the patent-based legal argument: > By open sourcing our DisplayLink technology for whatever personal reasons you may have as a "hobbyist," you will be single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology, which we have gone to great lengths and great expense to prevent. This sentence seems to be claiming that "DisplayLink's competitive advantage" is a *trade secret*. Patents don't protect trade secrets; in fact it's the opposite --- a patent is supposed to reveal your methods while giving you a monopoly over implementations of them. You could claim that some parts of your technology are patented and others are trade secrets, but you'd have to carefully lay out which parts are which, and the lawyer didn't do that here. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:46 UTC (Tue) by Cyberax ( ✭ supporter ✭ , #52523) [ Link ] Moreover, this is actually a ground for getting the patent revoked: "lack of enablement". synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:59 UTC (Tue) by wahern (subscriber, #37304) [ Link ] And any aspects that are trade secrets are fair-game for independent reverse engineering, anyhow. The lawyer is just saber rattling. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 12, 2026 3:04 UTC (Thu) by felixfix (subscriber, #242) [ Link ] You're both right: patents are supposed to describe something so clearly that it can be reproduced, but then it is illegal to do so. Pretty bizarre, to my mind. I despise intellectual property for other reasons, but I once worked up an alternate patent system which seemed fairer and might actually encourage its alleged justifications. From memory ... A patent includes: 1. The recipe to reproduce the object. 2. The royalty schedule. 3. A time limit. This can end in two ways: If no one reproduces the object within the time limit, the patent fails. If someone reproduces the object, the interval from patent to reproduction establishes the patent length. The incentives work out correctly: Inventors want as long a time limit as possible to get a longer patent. Inventors want as complex a patent as possible to prevent copycats. But if it's too complex and no one reproduces it, they have no patent. Copycats want to reproduce as soon as possible to get a shorter patent. Copycats may decide to reproduce it internally but not sell it, thus being ready to start selling the instant the time limit expires. There has to be some maximum time limit; otherwise inventors would choose 100 years. The multiplier from copycat time to patent length can be by legislative policy or vary per patent. (This is from memory. I may have forgotten some subtle aspects.) Free standard for USB displays is needed Posted Nov 11, 2026 16:02 UTC (Wed) by knewt (subscriber, #32124) [ Link ] (2 responses) So as I understand it, the point behind this displaylink tech, and the reason it's not using displayport, is that it allows you to connect more monitors than the graphics hardware in the computer actually supports. There is a piece of software that runs on the host computer, and acts as a virtual graphics card. The software then sends the display output (compressed in some way) over a regular usb data transport to the dock, which then converts that back into a regular display signal to be sent out over either an hdmi or displayport connector. Free standard for USB displays is needed Posted Nov 11, 2026 21:10 UTC (Wed) by rgmoore ( ✭ supporter ✭ , #75) [ Link ] (1 responses) My impression is this is mostly about the "compressed in some way" and "regular USB" parts. There might very well be legal problems producing a compatible FOSS implementation if their system uses patent-encumbered compression.
