Whatever they don’t cover is at best a trade secret, and reverse engineering a product you bought is generally a lawful way to learn one. Coke isn't suing the guy on YouTube who fastidiously reverse-engineered Coke. Either way, “showing people how it works” isn’t a harm patent law recognizes. It's a trade-secret grievance smuggled into a patent claim. Patented or secret? Posted Nov 11, 2026 19:13 UTC (Wed) by khim (subscriber, #9252) [ Link ] > I’m not a lawyer, but the complaint about “educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology” is hard to square with a patent claim. In an ideal world it would be immediate invalidation of the patent, because the whole point of patent is precisely to disclose such information — and if they fear that someone may disclose that valuable information then it means patent itself was bogus. In our world… no one cares. Even if it's supposed to invalidate the patent according to law, but in practice you need court decision for that and no one with deep enough pockets is interested in suing Synaptics. onsemi Posted Nov 11, 2026 20:21 UTC (Wed) by JanC_ (subscriber, #34940) [ Link ] Apparently onsemi now owns Synaptics (or at least announced they plan to own it, the process might not be over yet). Are they any better at open source? Wouldn't Be Infringement in USA Posted Nov 11, 2026 21:52 UTC (Wed) by linuxrocks123 (subscriber, #34648) [ Link ] (2 responses) First, I'm not a lawyer. I believe this to be true, but get actual advice or read the statute and come to your own conclusions. In the USA, patent infringement is covered under USC 271. There are several ways to infringe. Writing open source software isn't one of them: 271(a), direct infringement: Doesn't apply because you're not "making" or "selling" the entire invention. Are you "using" the invention? Well, I don't know: did you just write the code, or did you also run it in an infringing manner? And, if you did just write the code, if you're purely a hobbyist, the "experimental use" defense should cover you. If you do somehow lose on the experimental use exception, and they can prove it's willful, then oh God no! Treble damages! But you know how much treble damages would be for a single unit of a shit product like DisplayLink? Something like $0.60. So you'd probably be able to get the lawsuit thrown out of court based on the de minimis doctrine before it even got to trial. 271(b), inducement: Lots of ways this fails for the plaintiff. One way is that you have to actually talk to the person you're inducing to infringe. So, throw the code over the wall, talk only to other developers and not users, and you're good. 271(c), contributory: You have to sell or offer to sell it. You're not selling anything: you're giving your code away for free. Case closed. 2771(f), extraterritorial: There's a very nice case, Microsoft v. AT&T, where the facts were that Microsoft mailed a copy of Windows to a customer, on a CD or DVD or something like that, and AT&T said, "waaaah, Windoze is a component that infringes our patuntz, so you owe us under 271(f)!" and Microsoft said, "LOL GTFO luzer! Software's intangible and can't be a component of a patented invention!" The Supreme Court agreed with Microsoft. So, yeah, someone in the US should be good to pick up the torch here. Wouldn't Be Infringement in USA Posted Nov 12, 2026 1:25 UTC (Thu) by csamuel ( ✭ supporter ✭ , #2624) [ Link ] (1 responses) Isn't the US the wrong jurisdiction though? Mike Lothian is in Scotland, (currently) part of the UK. Wouldn't Be Infringement in USA Posted Nov 12, 2026 12:14 UTC (Thu) by linuxrocks123 (subscriber, #34648) [ Link ] Indeed he is, that's why I said, "Someone in the USA should be able to pick up the torch here." title: Your TV can see through walls (2025)
body_text: Your TV can see through walls: Navigation: Homepage      Index      Yearly archives Fun Astrophotography      (catalog) About this site Real pages Dark Light TTY Your TV can see through walls: 2025-08-02 — 2026-02-23 This is a spectogram of the signal from a local TV station: ATSC digital TV signal. (Recorded using an Ettus USRP B200) Walking between the receiver and TV station causes a slight disturbance to the signal, but it's nothing to write home about: Walking through the signal path For this capture, I moved the antenna a few centimeters: Where'd my signal go? This is selective fading : The direct signal is being canceled out by a strong reflection. Because the phase of the reflection depends on frequency, this effect is not uniform over the whole signal. Apart from being annoying if you're trying to watch TV, this state is extremely sensitive to any nearby movement. Here's what happened to the signal when I got up from my chair: ... and here's me walking around in a neighboring room: Stripes! The gaps between the stripes happen when my reflection perfectly cancels out the residual signal, which happens each time the path length changes by one wavelength. Let's use this to figure out how fast I was walking: The gap between each stripe is around 70 pixels, and the waterfall has an update rate of 150 Hz... 70 pixels * 1 second/150 pixels = 0.47 seconds = 2.1 Hz speed of light / 490 MHz * 2.1 Hz = 1.3 m/s = 4.6 km/h I was walking perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the speed can be used as is, without any adjustments for geometry. So, a simple radio reciever is able to detect motion and provide an estimated speed — and it's not just TV that works for this: any wideband radio signal like WiFi or LTE can be used in much the same way. Those make worse demonstrations because they have a messy waterfall, but it's possible extract the same data with a bit of work. Happy paranoia! Site wide RSS feed . Proudly supporting IPv6! AI usage generates a fragile codebase
body_text: AI usage generates a fragile codebase Evan X. Merz Programmer / Master Gardener / Doctor of Music / Curious Person AI usage generates a fragile codebase 2026-11-07,  Evan X. Merz programming , artificial intelligence , ai , llm , web programming I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it. I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers. Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame. In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications. By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop. Four ways AI makes codebases fragile Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase. 1. AI writes shallow tests One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric. 2. AI writes overly complex ccode AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand. 3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures. 4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code. Four signs that you have a fragile codebase If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase. 1. AI generated codebases have more incidents When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers. 2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve. 3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing. 4. AI results in a poor user experience And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification. Products made for humans require a human touch The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI. About me Buy my art

title: The Web Is More Than Enough
body_text: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford (Ftrain) Ftrain , by Paul Ford Home / Publications / Print, Web, and Newsletters / The Aboard Newsletter Oct 21, 2026 The Aboard Newsletter The Web Is More Than Enough Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be. You can have it all, my empire of alert(). Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com —you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.”  So many people visited that the server went down (well, I maxxed out the CloudFlare free plan), and ultimately, after I put in my credit card, a couple hundred thousand people came by to check it out. People on Hacker News insisted it was a pointless waste of time, and folks on GitHub started asking for features and fixes, all of which we’re considering, and some of which we’re doing. The Register wrote an article about it , and it also made it, for a little while, to the top ten of Product Hunt . So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this: The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications. I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement:  The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day. I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too. Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there. The Web Crypto API is a first-class security platform in the browser. The Web Assembly platform lets you run native-speed code in your browser. WebGL provides for high-quality 3D and 2D graphics in your browser. The Web Audio API lets you mix sound in your browser. And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it. I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line. My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones . He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline. Time to place your Fab Plant. As he wrote about it : … but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build! All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL.  The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane. This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like?  This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be. It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side. title: Horible public key tricks
body_text: Horrible public key tricks: Navigation: Homepage      Index      Yearly archives Fun Astrophotography      (catalog) About this site Real pages Dark Light TTY Horrible public key tricks: 2026-11-08 — 2026-11-09 So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server. ... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4" There is prior art of protest SSL implementations , but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate. The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it. A good protest should be obvious: # openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com : 443 /dev/null \ | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color= yes -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year///// DSfCAfXcsJfBpnHekS0qnf5YLl c54VuUNRVINcDkEwJDwyB96+xE/uXhtiGdk8ty1PF6jciLEYCJBHcmqOa5pOyV8m 63yR3NE6hCQlaSLQQDo96Sb0/10aC5LqE7KwEskrP/qeCzT7vDN7fh+dXOGs+VMw CERTIFICATE----- First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent. The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent: # Encryption requires knowing e (public) cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q. # Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) = cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext --> Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there. The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus. My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p. The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176 (incrementing until the next prime...) 58174124 * 9184918 43 = 5343245836 7670532 As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner. From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: # Single domain openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request # Wildcard cat > config <<EOF [ req ] req_extensions = req_ext [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.example.com DNS.2 = example.com EOF openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request ... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts. The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated. Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) available charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice. As for security , this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key. A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys. The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.
